SNEAK PEEK

— Health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein, with calls for Europe to be better prepared to protect health infrastructure. 

— Parliament’s environment committee backs an opinion on the Biotech Act supporting a one-year patent extension. 

— Europe’s response to the U.S. most-favored-nation policy was a hot topic at Gastein, with France’s new pharma deal stealing the spotlight.

Welcome to Friday’s Morning Health Care! It’s been a big week at Gastein and it only cost attendees a bout of food poisoning, burnout and one unlucky Italian getting lost in the woods, spending the night by a waterfall before being rescued by helicopter. This year also bids farewell to Clemens Martin Auer, who hands over the Gastein presidency to Nick Fahy, director of the health and care research group at RAND Europe.

Mark your calendars: Our weekly health care calendar lands in your inbox on Thursday. You can also go online to export and plan your week or suggest your own event. 

Get in touch: cchiappa@politico.eu, dgiannini@politico.eu. Follow us on X: @chiappa_claudia, @domgiannini_  

DRIVING THE DAY

GEAR UP: Europe needs to better prepare to protect health infrastructure, delegates heard, as health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein.

Spread out: Petter Iversen, chair of NATO’s Committee of the Chiefs of Military Medical Services, said there were different ways Europe could protect health infrastructure, which continues to be under attack in Ukraine. “You can spread things out, use a larger geographical area and hide things,” he told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of the conference.

Hiding hospitals: One option is to move hospitals into underground facilities to protect them from attacks, he said. “When we are building infrastructures in the future … we might have to think about dual use. If you’re building a parking cellar, maybe you should have enough power or electricity, and also water supplies, so you can actually build a kind of hospital in there.”

Eastern Europe is already experiencing increasing threats from Russia, with drones and cyberattacks now frequent events, Iversen said. Countries closer to Russia had good plans in place, he said. “Situational awareness is sharper closer to the eastern flank,” he said. “You feel the pressure on a daily basis.” 

Where we’re vulnerable: European pharmaceuticals and production are also at risk since supply chains are dependent on countries like China, he said. “We need to prepare to reduce our dependencies from whom we will not want to be dependent upon if it comes to a major crisis.” 

Prepare for everything: The health care system needed to be resilient enough to withstand shocks, including those that went beyond war, like earthquakes, summer heatwaves or cyberattacks putting stress on the sector, said Jarno Habicht, the World Health Organization’s outgoing representative in Ukraine. “You might have more patients, but you might be also without electricity, so we need to be ready for the shocks,” he told Morning Health Care. 

Read more about what Iversen and Habicht said on health security and Ukraine here.

INFORMAL MEETING: Health ministers met in Dublin on Thursday where they discussed tobacco and nicotine pouches, the Biotech Act, medical devices reform and cardiovascular health.

On Aug. 4, a drone struck the wing of a Ukrainian aircraft at Germany’s Leipzig Airport and fell onto the tarmac. Strapped beneath it was a tin can packed with explosives. The device remained intact.

That gave investigators something unusually valuable: the bomb itself. The can was sealed with a metal plate stamped with seven circular indentations, according to an investigative file from German federal police reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.

It wasn’t the first time such an improvised explosive had been discovered on European soil. Almost two years earlier, on Aug. 20, 2024, police investigators arrived at a cemetery in Kaunas, Lithuania, with a bomb disposal team. They had received a highly sensitive tip from Poland concerning explosives and a Ukrainian man alleged to have deposited them there for Russian intelligence, according to investigation files from the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau.

At a weathered grave, beneath artificial flowers and concrete slabs, officers recovered a plastic bag containing two tin cans. According to their labels, they contained corn. Forensic analysis, however, found they contained 968 grams of explosives, around 700 grams of TNT equivalent per can — roughly the lethal force of four hand grenades. 

In January and June 2025, investigators unearthed more explosive-filled cans at various locations in Lithuania. Four were fitted with metal plates stamped with circular indentations. Investigators say they were intended to act as projectiles in an explosion. Forensic examinations found that the plates were highly likely to have been manufactured by the same machine, according to a report by the Forensic Science Service of the Police Department of Lithuania.

The device attached to the drone in Leipzig bore striking similarities to those recovered from the Lithuanian caches, including the explosive-filled tin can and the stamped metal plate.

The resemblance alone does not establish that the devices belonged to the same operation. But two Western security officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss security matters, say it fits with other evidence — including travel records, suspected logistics routes and intelligence reporting — linking the cases to a broader Russian intelligence mission.

The resemblance is one element of a pattern that German and European officials believe points to an escalating campaign of sabotage and violence across Europe, planned and coordinated by Russian intelligence officers.

According to three senior German and European security officials, the main driver of the campaign is Russia’s GRU military intelligence service. At its core, they say, is Unit 29155 — a military intelligence outfit linked to destabilization operations in European countries. 

German authorities say they expect further “hybrid” operations as Russian President Vladimir Putin seeks to disrupt military support for Ukraine and raise the political cost of backing Kyiv. 

“The population is supposed to fear a direct military confrontation and therefore question the purpose of supporting Ukraine,” said Gerhard Schindler, former president of Germany’s BND Federal Intelligence Service. “That is why he will increase both the military pressure on Ukraine and the hybrid pressure on the West.”

In response to an inquiry, the Russian Embassy in Berlin denied any Russian involvement in acts of sabotage in Europe. “We firmly reject the baseless allegations concerning Russia’s purported involvement in the alleged ‘drone incident’ at Leipzig Airport, as well as in other ‘sabotage activities,’” a spokesperson said.

Russian connection

One of the clearest trails leads to Oleg Levushkin, a dual Latvian-Russian national whom German authorities suspect of helping prepare the Leipzig attack. According to a senior German security official and investigative files reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, Levushkin is not a low-level recruit but a GRU-linked logistics operative with longstanding ties to senior figures in Russian military intelligence. 

On social media, Levushkin offers glimpses of a seemingly ordinary life: motorcycle trips to Crimea and the Hungarian-Serbian border, a visit to Volgograd’s Motherland Calls statue, and time spent fishing, skiing and travelling across Europe with his family. The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network reviewed his profiles on the social media sites VKontakte and Odnoklassniki.

According to one German intelligence official and documents related to the case, investigators believe Levushkin traveled via Turkey to Berlin Brandenburg Airport in late July to prepare the Leipzig operation. He rented a car there on July 27, according to location data mentioned in German investigation files. Investigators believe the explosives entered Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia in the cavities of long-haul trucks, according to the senior official from Germany.

On July 31, the rental car was recorded near Leipzig Airport, where investigators believe he was carrying out reconnaissance ahead of the attempted attack, according to documents from the investigation. Levushkin did not reply to a request for comment.

Levushkin’s alleged links reach into the upper ranks of Russian military intelligence. According to reporting by German media as well as the London-based non-profit Dossier Center, he has maintained a close relationship for roughly two decades with GRU Colonel Denis Smolyaninov.

A December 2025 report by the State Security Department of Lithuania says Smolyaninov is “the head of the GRU’s Ukraine department, specializes in psychological operations and is linked to covert sabotage campaigns organized in Europe using the social network Telegram.” 

According to the 2025 intelligence report, Smolyaninov also coordinated the activities of the Russian-linked private military company Longifolia, registered in Panama. European investigators suspect several shareholders in the company of involvement in an operation where incendiary devices were sent to Poland and Britain, according to Lithuanian investigation files. One of the parcels caught fire on July 20, 2024 while being transferred at Leipzig Airport. Another ignited two days later in Birmingham, England. 

Lithuanian intelligence explicitly attributes the parcel operation to the GRU, and in particular to Unit 29155. A November 2025 dossier by Lithuania’s State Security Department reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network describes the unit as being “tasked with carrying out killings, operations to destroy infrastructure, disrupting the activities of institutions that run counter to Russia’s interests, and terrorist attacks in Western countries.” 

Its agents, the November 2025 dossier says, are “trained in handling explosives and firearms [and] can identify human sources and build agent networks.”

Unit 29155 has previously been linked by Western governments and investigators to a series of operations across Europe, including explosions at ammunition depots in Bulgaria and the Czech Republic and the 2018 poisoning of former Russian spy Sergei Skripal in Britain, according to the dossier. The Lithuanian dossier also links the unit to more recent arson attacks, including at an Ikea store in Vilnius and a post office in Bucharest.

The Russian government’s press service did not respond to a request for comment about GRU Unit 29155 and Smolyaninov.

German officials have blamed the GRU for a failed incendiary attack on a defense company in Munich in September, while Estonia’s intelligence service said this week in a public statement that an August arson attack on defense company Milrem Robotics had been commissioned by Russian intelligence.

European security authorities interviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network expect such operations to increase in the coming months, with defense companies, critical infrastructure and people involved in supporting Ukraine among the potential targets.

The Kremlin views its relationship with Europe as a “systemic conflict,” said Omar Haijawi-Pirchner, the former head of Austria’s domestic intelligence service. Like others interviewed for this article, he said he expects an increase in drone incursions and hybrid attacks.

“We believe that Russia is currently under remarkably high pressure — probably higher than at any previous point during the war and at any time during Vladimir Putin’s tenure,” said a senior NATO official who was granted anonymity to discuss security matters. 

“From the Kremlin’s point of view, the best option available to them seems to be to intensify the hybrid campaign they are waging against the West,” the official added.

POLITICO reported in June that Street was seen as a leading candidate for the first chair of Great British Railways, which will oversee rail infrastructure and services as part of Labour’s reversal of the Conservative rail privatization three decades ago.

He was interviewed for the role but Labour ministers will not hand it to him, according to two people with knowledge of the decision, both of whom were granted anonymity to speak frankly. One suggested the decision was mutual.

Both of the people said a key reason was that Street still appeared to harbor a desire to return to frontline politics. One of the people, a government official, said he had been “unable to subdue his political ambitions.” Street was the Conservative mayor of the West Midlands for seven years until Labour narrowly defeated him in 2024.

Street declined to comment on the Great British Railways recruitment process, and told POLITICO that supposition about his political intentions was “speculation” and “conjecture.”

Recruitment began in January for the role of chair, which will pay £200,000 to £300,000 a year for 10 days of work a month. Great British Railways is due to be up and running in 2027, with passenger services transferred to public ownership by the end of that year as private rail operators’ contracts expire.

The Department for Transport declined to comment on whether a decision was imminent or the process of finding a chair had slowed. A government official said a “fair, open and merit-based process” was underway.

Street has history with Britain’s railways. He narrowly decided not to quit the Conservatives in 2023 when former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak scrapped a leg of the planned High Speed 2 rail line from Birmingham to Manchester.

Supporters describe him as a figure who reached across political lines and was respected for his nine-year stint as managing director of department store John Lewis.

The job of West Midlands mayor — who holds one of the largest single electoral mandates of any British politician — will come up for election again in 2028. 

Street has continued to make appearances around the region, including visiting the scene of wildfires outside Birmingham over summer. He also has a busy schedule at the Conservative Party Conference this weekend in the same city, including with the center-right policy network Prosper which he co-founded with former Scottish Conservatives Leader Ruth Davidson.

Prominent Conservatives from the center-right flank have, however, been blocked from the party’s list of candidates for the next general election, expected by 2029. Party Leader Kemi Badenoch has insisted that future candidates must agree to abandoning net zero carbon policies and to withdrawing from the European Convention on Human Rights.

A person who has worked with Street said he was “building up a campaign and keeping key relationships alive,” and that any move by the party to block him from running on a Conservative ticket if he chose to would be “a ridiculous act of self-harm.”

Street said it would be wrong to draw any conclusions about his future ambitions in frontline politics. “This is pure political speculation with two and two making five,” he said. “It is true that I will be active at conference as co-chair of ProsperUK making the case for moderate Conservatism, and demonstrating the support our movement has. 

“It is also true that I remain deeply committed to the West Midlands. It is my home and I will continue to dedicate time and energy to its future. But the idea that these two facts are part of a wider plan is just conjecture.”

]]> en Burnham wants to change British elections. Voters think they’re fine already. https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-burnham-change-british-elections-voters-poll/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 02 Oct 2026 02:02:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9094796 LONDON — Andy Burnham has his work cut out to convince voters the U.K. should change the way it elects MPs, according to a new POLITICO Poll. 

This week the prime minister vowed to come up with proposals to ditch the first-past-the-post voting system, which has been used in British general elections since 1884, to provide more political stability and a system that is fairer to all voters. 

But a survey by pollsters Public First, conducted before Burnham’s announcement, found that 57% of respondents regard first-past-the-post as a “mostly” or “completely” fair way to decide elections. (A majority of voters across parties feel this way.) 

At the same time, the survey revealed potential openness to a system of proportional representation, in which the number of parliamentary seats each party wins is more closely linked to the total number of votes it receives across the country. 

“Most people don’t spend much time thinking about how we elect MPs and, broadly, people think the current system is fair,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at Public First. “Burnham will need to make a convincing case to voters about why changing the electoral system is necessary, if he is to gain support for his plans.” 

Under first-past-the-post, whichever candidate wins the most votes in their constituency is elected to represent that seat, even if they fall far short of a majority of local voters. Nationally, that can result in a party taking power with relatively low popular support.

Labour won the last election in 2024 by a landslide, taking 63% of seats in Parliament with just 34% of the vote — the most disproportionate result in British history. 

Since then, some polling projections have suggested Nigel Farage’s populist-right Reform UK party was on track to win a majority with around 30% of votes under the first-past-the-post system. 

In a speech to Labour members in Liverpool, Burnham said recent turbulence in British politics — he’s the country’s seventh prime minister in 10 years — meant a new system was needed. “We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No. 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote,” he said. 

How to choose

Many voting systems could replace first-past-the-post, some based on a form of proportional representation (PR). Public First’s analysis found that support for moving to PR varied depending on which party was proposing it. 

When Labour voters were shown a Labour proposal to move to PR, 54% supported the idea, whereas when they were shown an identical proposal branded as coming from Reform UK, only 36% supported it. The same broad pattern was true of Reform voters. 

Overall, 41% of U.K. adults responding to the poll said they would “somewhat” support or “strongly support” a Labour proposal to move toward PR. Another 26% would neither support nor oppose it, and 22% somewhat opposed or strongly opposed the idea. 

“While they lean toward supporting reform, many voters judge it by who is proposing it,” said Wride. “With trust in politicians so low, if electoral reform looks like just one party’s project, it risks being seen as political game-playing.” 

Burnham’s pledge on electoral reform could boost his chances of staying in power, but much could change ahead of the next election, which could take place as late as 2029. Polls currently predict a hung parliament with Labour falling short of a majority, but the Liberal Democrats have long campaigned for electoral reform and would be Labour’s most likely coalition partners. 

Farage has also spoken in favor of replacing first-past-the-post with an alternative voting system, but has recently said less on the topic. This week, the party’s deputy leader Richard Tice said it was “no time” to be discussing electoral reform.

One person familiar with the thinking in Burnham’s team said they expected the government preference would be for the same “supplementary vote” system used in Greater Manchester mayoral elections. It allows voters to pick a second preference — with those votes being counted if the lead candidate doesn’t win at least 50% of first preference votes. 

Separately, a government official said a “constituency link” in any new voting system would be “critical” for Burnham.

“I found it better being elected under a different system as mayor of Greater Manchester where people had one or two — they could put that on the ballot paper,” Burnham told the BBC this week. “Because you had a reason to stop on every doorstep and chat to people who might not always support your party and try and get their second preference. It just led to a better politics.”

Sam Blewett and Emilio Casalicchio contributed reporting. Public First surveyed 2,028 U.K. adults online Sept. 13-15, 2026.

Europe war-games life after Merz

The German chancellor’s foes at home are rejoicing at his political downturn. But those in Brussels aren’t.

By GABRIEL GAVIN and FRIDA PREUß

Illustration by Natália Delgado/ POLITICO

The EU can’t pretend Friedrich Merz isn’t in trouble any longer.

After a string of humiliating election losses where the far right has made historic gains and an internal fight with his own coalition over social care policy, EU partners are starting to plan for the prospect that the German chancellor could be ousted — or at least distracted — in the crucial coming months, according to five diplomats and officials who spoke to POLITICO. They were granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive talks.

Two European governments have even held internal sessions to game out what the end of Merz’s chancellorship would mean for EU policymaking, two of those familiar with the discussions said.

It’s not a prospect they take lightly. Merz leads the EU’s largest economy and is the chief negotiator for wealthy countries seeking to rein in spending in the bloc’s proposed €2 trillion seven-year budget. He is also a driving force behind EU efforts to save heavy industry.

“Any debate about the German chancellor weakens Germany’s role in the EU and in the world,” said Wilhelm Gebhard, a member of the Bundestag and an official in Merz’s governing CDU party.

With France facing its own far-right surge and a presidential election next year that could hand power to euroskeptic Marine Le Pen, few in Brussels relish the prospect of Germany, historically the EU’s other major player, turning inwards or derailing important negotiations.

The contingency planning, which has seen officials and diplomats brainstorm the situation, comes after months of mixed signals from Berlin on EU policy, including car emissions and a proposed social media ban for children. Even if Merz stays in office, the political turmoil is already complicating Berlin’s work on the EU’s biggest files.

The worst-case scenario for Brussels would be a leaderless Germany, or one with a far-right government. But that is seen as virtually impossible in the short term, with none of the mainstream players seeking new elections while the far-right Alternative for Germany party are leading in the polls.

“All coalition partners know that they have a great deal to lose from early elections,” said Hannah Neumann, an opposition Green MEP who sits on the European Parliament’s security and foreign affairs committees. “My expectation, therefore, is that they will stay together and muddle through.”

While Merz himself could be forced to resign in the face of his growing unpopularity, he would be replaced straight away by a successor from either his center-right CDU party or his center-left coalition partner, the SPD. That should give Brussels confidence “someone will always be in charge,” said one of the diplomats.

For more polling data from across Europe visit POLITICO Poll of Polls.

Searching for a win

Those who know him insist Merz won’t be distracted when it comes to EU affairs.

“Other politicians might say ‘OK, I focus less on EU politics.’ For him it’s just the opposite: It’s an additional incentive to show leadership in Europe,” said a person familiar with the chancellor’s thinking.

In the immediate term, Merz’s political weakness at home could make finding compromise on the bloc’s next seven-year budget harder by pushing the chancellor to double down on Berlin’s hardline stance in search of a win, a further two diplomats warned.

As the leading voice for countries seeking a smaller EU budget, which leaders hope to agree by year-end, Merz has called for cuts of “hundreds of billions of euros.” Germany, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Austria and the Netherlands are pressing for overall reductions, while net recipients such as Poland and Romania want to protect their share.

Nobody who could replace him as chancellor “would be able to be more flexible than Merz is,” said one of the diplomats, but “the risk is he has to show his self-perceived leadership in Brussels in the hope it will help his standing in Germany.”

An envoy from another country said “domestically he is weak [which means] he can’t compromise” and needs to be seen to score a win by slashing the budget as far as possible.

But Merz’s allies say his fight on the world stage is only worthwhile if his coalition partners play along behind the curtain.

“Strength comes not just from grand appearances in Brussels, but above all from stability, reliability and the ability to push through decisions at home. That is precisely what is lacking at the moment,” said CDU Bundestag member Fabian Gramling. “Germany’s influence in Europe also depends on how united and capable of action the federal government appears at home.”

Infighting and indecision

The fractious relationship between the CDU and the SPD has already been undercutting Berlin’s stance on issues of critical national importance.

Throughout 2025, as Brussels renegotiated a planned phaseout of combustion engine cars, in the face of fierce lobbying from Germany’s influential automotive sector, German officials and diplomats were unable to articulate a clear position, with center-right ministers wanting to scrap the green policy and their center-left counterparts pushing to preserve it.

Ultimately Merz’s fellow German conservatives in Brussels — Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European People’s Party chief Manfred Weber — stepped in to kill the proposal at the eleventh hour.

Another key policy area where the coalition struggled to agree a position was on whether children should be banned from social media, a flagship EU-wide proposal from von der Leyen. While Merz personally backed the idea at the start of the year, he and his political allies spent more than six months struggling to land on a specific age limit to lobby for when von der Leyen was consulting with partners, according to officials and diplomats involved in the talks.

Even before the latest crisis, Merz’s domestic troubles were spilling into Brussels at the highest level. Last year, he surprised fellow EU leaders by demanding that a summit scheduled to cover geopolitics and other policy files should instead focus on saving European heavy industry from competition with the U.S. and China.

Germany lost around 124,100 industrial jobs last year, according to an analysis by EY, with the government concerned deindustrialization is helping drive support for Merz’s far-right and far-left rivals. Other capitals share his concerns, but Merz has insisted industry should top the agenda at future summits.

But even inside the chancellor’s own CDU, he has struggled to achieve consensus on what to do about it. As the Commission plans a push against unfair Chinese trade practices, Merz’s fellow party member and foreign minister Katherina Reiche is seen as more protective over the relationship with Beijing, and the German industrial giants like Volkswagen and BASF that trade with it.

In a speech on Thursday commemorating 36 years of German reunification — the fall of the Berlin Wall and the dissolution of communist East Germany —the country’s ambassador to the EU, Thomas Ossowski, told fellow envoys and officials that “whenever we celebrate German unity, we celebrate European unity. And we need this unity [now] more than ever.”

Gabriel Gavin reported from Brussels. Frida Preuß reported from Berlin. Jordyn Dahl, Eliza Gkritsi and Carlo Martuscelli contributed to this report.

But the EU’s top trade official also emphasized the political pressure he is under to find that elusive common ground with Beijing. “I feel high political interest and, of course, very high expectations from the leaders all across the European Union,” Šefčovič said in an interview on the sidelines of a meeting of G20 trade ministers in Milwaukee.

“I know how politically impatient the European leadership is.”

Šefčovič travels to Beijing Oct. 8 for what he termed a “a super crucial meeting” with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, and said he was optimistic the trip will bear fruit. “You have to believe that you can accomplish something, otherwise you better don’t go.”

The commissioner needs to get results he can present at a meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Oct. 15-16, and has said previously that Brussels is ready to restrict Chinese access to the EU market should the talks fail.

The EU and China have been locked in tense negotiations since June. EU leaders have said they can no longer tolerate the flood of Chinese imports inundating the single market, putting pressure on domestic manufacturers and forcing plant closures and layoffs.

“I think our Chinese partners understood that this has direct implication on the future of emblematic European companies — literally thousands of jobs,” Šefčovič reported. “And also the social fabric and social model which was developed in Europe over many, many decades.”

The bloc’s ballooning €1-billion-a-day trade deficit with China lies at the heart of the talks. Cutting that deficit would require either reducing imports from China, boosting EU exports, or a mix of the two.

Šefčovič said he hopes to bring a “proof of concept” back from Beijing that addresses three main issues: sudden Chinese export surges in key industrial sectors; tangible ways to increase European goods exports to China; and long-term clarity regarding China’s export curbs on raw materials, especially rare earth elements.

While in Milwaukee, Šefčovič met with Chinese Vice-Minister Li Chenggang. The veteran Slovak commissioner said China understands Europe’s worries: “All the issues we suggested are on the table. I’m not saying that we have clear-cut reassurances that we will solve them, but they are on the table.”

“Some of these topics have been very difficult to put on the agenda in the past. I believe this reflects the understanding of how politically important this is for both of us.”

The bilateral consultations have been divided into four work streams: trade and investment balancing; export controls; intellectual property rights; and reform of the World Trade Organization.

One person with knowledge of the negotiations, who asked to remain anonymous due to the sensitivity of the talks, said the Commission was seeking a settlement with China that would involve a mix of bilateral agreements on certain product categories, coupled with unilateral restrictions on others.

The Commission will present the outcome of the negotiations to EU leaders at their mid-October meeting in Brussels. The leaders will then decide whether the results are satisfactory.

French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday criticized China for unfairly subsidizing its domestic producers and urged the Commission to deploy more safeguards to protect European industry.

China has also signaled that it’s ready to fight back. Responding to an as-yet-unpublished Franco-German position paper that is expected to urge an upgrade to the EU’s trade defenses, a spokesperson for the Commerce Ministry said China would take “firm action” against any moves to restrict goods from entering the European single market.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Fri, 02 Oct 2026 08:16:58 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.2 Listen: Are EU countries allowed to bring back border controls whenever they want? https://euobserver.com/240734/listen-are-eu-countries-allowed-to-bring-back-border-controls-whenever-they-want/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 08:16:58 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240734 Italy brought back border controls with Spain in August, and has now extended them until at least 15 October, as more EU countries introduce checks.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 

Italy brought back border controls with Spain in August, and has now extended them until at least 15 October. Giorgia Meloni’s government fears that migrants who arrived in Ceuta, reach the continent and Italy.

Are these restrictions legal in the Schengen area? What are the EU’s levies to avoid such controls?

Since 1 August, Italy has temporarily reintroduced controls at its air and sea borders with Spain. The measure has now been extended until 15 October. In return, Spain has also introduced controls at its air and sea borders with Italy.

Read more

[Interview] Ceuta crisis shows how EU border outsourcing puts children at risk, says German lawyer

“This is not against Spain” the Italian foreign affairs minister Antonio Tajani said, adding “we have a duty to protect our borders.”

The starting point was the arrival of tens of thousands of migrants in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July. Italy said it was concerned about possible secondary movements towards the rest of Europe, and brought back controls at its borders with Spain.

But from a legal point of view, EU countries can’t simply reintroduce border controls whenever they want.

The Schengen area is based on the principle of free movement, meaning there should normally be no checks at internal borders. The Schengen Borders Code provides an exception. If a country faces a serious threat to public policy or internal security, it can temporarily reintroduce border controls, as a measure of last resort.

The controls can initially be introduced for up to 30 days, and can then be extended under certain conditions.

Read more

THIS WEEK: Interior ministers discuss Fortress Europe, as Kallas goes to Syria

Italy has already extended its measure, which has now been in place for more than two months.

What does the European Commission say about Italy’s decision? The Commission has been asked about the Italian controls and says it is currently assessing the situation.

But the Brussels-based organisation The Good Lobby argues that Italy is violating the Schengen rules. It filed a complaint with the European Commission, asking it to open an infringement procedure against Italy.

According to Alberto Alemanno, who filed the complaint, there is no security threat that would justify bringing back the controls.

His argument is that none of the migrants who arrived in Ceuta were transferred to Italy. And, he says, people travelling between Ceuta and mainland Spain are already subject to identity checks.

So Italy’s justification, he argues, does not meet the conditions set out in the Schengen Borders Code.

Now, is Italy the only EU country bringing back border controls? No. If you look at the notifications sent by EU countries to the European Commission, around ten countries have reported temporary controls at some of their internal borders in recent months.

Read more

EU’s new cross‑border work rules favour recruitment, not workers, say critics

In response to the situation in Ceuta, Italy is the main example.

Austria also notified the Commission of controls in September, citing the situation in Ceuta among several reasons. But those controls concern its land borders with Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovenia.

So Austria is not checking passengers arriving by air from Spain.

Germany, for example, has invoked the same exception in the Schengen rules to carry out controls at its land borders with all its neighbours.

That does not mean that every border crossing is closed, or that every traveller is systematically checked. It means German authorities can carry out checks at those borders, including spot checks.

Germany’s main justification is continued migratory pressure, alongside other security concerns. And for now, the Commission is kind of letting all of this happen. It did raise concerns at some point: in June, the Commission published an assessment of temporary border controls in nine EU countries, including Germany, Austria and Italy.

It did not formally declare these countries’ controls illegal. Instead, it called on them to work towards lifting the controls, arguing that the EU has put in place measures to address some of the risks being invoked to justify them.

Those measures include the new Migration and Asylum Pact and new rules on entry and border management. The bigger question, then, is how long temporary border controls can remain in place before they stop being an exception to Schengen and become the new normal.

From Rome to Budapest, governments have been rolling back the progress, with initiatives stalling all the way up to EU level. ]]> Europeans have lead the field on access to abortion, but a conservative comeback has caused a lot of those advances to regress.

Research published earlier this week (28 September) by the Centre for Reproductive Rights (CRR) found that despite an upward trend of legalisation, some countries are still seeking to enforce barriers and rolling back entitlement to abortion care.

This resistance to change is also evidenced in the lack of member state participation in safe abortion funds available since the the ‘My Voice, My Choice’ European citizens’ initiative for safe and accessible abortion was passed into law last February. 

EU funds could since then be used to create regional programmes for safe abortion care for anyone who can’t access it in their own country, as well as financing travel to a country where abortion is available.

However, no funds have yet been used.

A Mamdani moment could happen, since people feel that politics has exhausted itself.]]> “Marine Le Pen has reinvented herself. Her style now is more moderate,” reckons Jacques Rupnik, a French political scientist, ahead of the country’s widely anticipated battle for the presidency.

Many voters in France will vote for the candidate they see as having the best chance of defeating the far-right leader, Rupnik explains.

“All polls show that if the far-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon faced Marine Le Pen in the second round of France’s presidential election, Marine Le Pen would win,” he says, explaining that many French votes are unwilling to back Mélenchon.

In his interview with Denník N, Rupnik claims Mélenchon is the first French presidential candidate to seek support from immigrants so explicitly.

Find out:

  • How Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon have used the migration debate for their campaigns.
  • Why the presidential frontrunners do not understand economic issues.
  • Rupnik’s assessment of Emmanuel Macron’s two presidential terms.

Polls suggest that if France held a presidential election now, far-right Marine Le Pen and far-left Mélenchon would make the second round. What does this tell us about France?

France is divided and polarised. Young people in particular tend to lean towards more radical parties. Establishment parties are old and worn; they have lost their appeal. In French presidential elections there are two rounds. In the first round, you vote for your preferred candidate; in the second, you vote for the lesser evil. The balance has shifted, and right-wing voters are saying: “Why should we, the right, be excluded from politics simply because Macron has failed and the Le Pen has grown stronger?”

Immigration is another reason behind growing support for Le Pen. Mélenchon is also capitalising on the immigration debate, but in the opposite way to her.

Mélenchon opposes Le Pen’s position by arguing that immigrants integrate. “Mélenchon has therefore adopted the theory of grand remplacement, but instead of presenting it as a threat, he has turned it into a huge opportunity.”

And Mélenchon argues that it is fine for immigrants to remain in their own communities, practise their own religions, for women to wear headscarves and so on.

The great replacement conspiracy theory (“grand remplacement“) should be mentioned since the far right embraced it long ago. It is the idea that the native French population will gradually be replaced by new immigrants.

And Mélenchon now says: “What great replacement? On the contrary, it is an opportunity for France. He says: “The more of us there are, the better.”

Mélenchon has therefore adopted the theory of grand remplacement, but instead of presenting it as a threat, he has turned it into a huge opportunity. Of course, everyone knows what he is aiming for. It is an election campaign, and he is appealing to voters who are themselves immigrants.

Previously, no one focused on immigrants in elections except Le Pen who used them as a bogeyman. And now Mélenchon says: “We are appealing to Muslims.” He says Muslim headscarves are fine and religious symbols are fine. He says anyone who opposes this is racist.

Donald Trump is betting on voluntary commitments from AI companies. On Tuesday (29 September), he unveiled a self-regulatory agreement drawn up with some of the biggest names in the AI industry.

What does it mean, and how does it differ from the EU’s Code of Practice for general-purpose AI?

On Tuesday, September 29, Trump brought together the CEOs of some of the biggest AI companies. Together, they signed what could be described as a self-regulation pact: a short list of non-binding commitments called the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

So, what exactly have these companies committed to? The CEOs of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, SpaceX and Nvidia have pledged to put safeguards in place, quickly detect and fix problems, and have their systems checked by independent auditors.

The principle of voluntary commitments may sound familiar to Europeans: They echo the EU’s Code of Practice for general-purpose AI — which, like the White House agreement, is not legally binding.

And, more importantly, the EU does have binding rules in place: the AI Act, which is already in force. As part of this regulation, the European Commission developed the Code of Practice to help companies comply with the rules.

There are binding obligations under the AI Act. But they are not as precise as what is in the code of conduct.

The United States has generally been less inclined towards binding regulation of the sector. Trump has argued that rules can hinder the development of companies, and has promoted a national framework that is as minimally restrictive as possible.

The White House document does leave the door open to legislation in the future. It says that, over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into lows or regulations.

Today, policymakers backed by big polluters are betraying that promise in the name of “competitiveness”. 

In June 2026, Florence, Franck, and Isabelle packed their bags and headed to Brussels. Why? Because their children have all suffered serious harm from pesticides. 

These children have endured physical pain and heavy medical procedures, including repeated chemotherapy treatments. And their families have shouldered both the financial and emotional burdens alongside them.

As Isabelle puts it: “It destroys a family.” Her own daughter has been fighting leukaemia for the last seven years.

And they are not alone. In 2024, almost one in 20 children in the EU were exposed to dangerous levels of pesticides; that’s 380,000 kids. Now these parents have a clear message for policymakers: prioritise public health and stop dismantling the rules that protect children against harmful substances. 

In 2024, around 316,000 tonnes of toxic pesticides were sold in the EU to be sprayed across our countryside, risking not only the health of farmers but also polluting our soil, air and water.  

The European Environment Agency in Copenhagen has reported environmentally unsafe levels of pesticides in about a quarter of Europe’s rivers. In groundwater – which supplies 65 percent of the water we drink in Europe – unsafe levels were detected in 11-18 percent of water bodies. 

In the same year, trifluoroacetic acid, a harmful “forever chemical” that forms when ‘PFAS’ pesticides and F-gases break down, showed up in 94 percent of drinking water samples tested across 11 EU countries.

In December 2025, the European Commission proposed a legislative package that would remove fundamental environmental and health protections against pesticides in the EU.

Among other changes, the proposal – ironically labelled the ‘Food and Feed Safety’ Omnibus – suggests extending pesticide approvals indefinitely and relaxing the rules to allow pesticides already identified as hazardous to remain on the EU market. 

Let that sink in, no pun intended.

These proposals are a political choice to prioritise short-term profits for Big Polluters over children’s lives, people’s health, and the nature and ecosystems we need to survive.

Human health is at stake, and children are at particular risk – as they absorb substances more easily and are less able to excrete them. 

Pesticide exposure is linked to the development of childhood cancers, hormone disruption, neurodevelopmental impairments and birth defects. And prenatal and early childhood exposure can permanently alter development, with consequences that can be irreversible – and deadly.  

Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, as well as the UN-declared human right to a healthy environment, all EU countries must commit to protecting children from environmental harm and ensure the highest attainable standard of health.

These principles must guide the work of EU institutions. 

Yet, instead of strengthening protections, the EU is moving backwards at a worrying speed. This is largely due to intense (and repeated) lobbying from multi-billion euro corporations, which includes the pesticides industry. Corporate chemical giants now spend €46m a year just to lobby the EU; that’s over 60 percent more than in 2020. 

Make it make sense

The incoherence of current EU policy is troubling. On the one hand, the EU Commission is celebrating its new Intergenerational Fairness Strategy – a framework that is meant to ensure today’s policies do not disadvantage future generations. On the other, the same institution is actively seeking to relax controls of harmful substances. 

Ripping up rules that protect people and the planet only benefits Big Polluters, industries that already make billions in profits at the expense of children’s health.

What’s more, an independent assessment found that the measures the EU institutions propose “will not accelerate innovations and authorisations”. In short, these proposals would actually make Europe less competitive.

Children’s rights and youth organisations have warned that deregulation exposes children to serious (and preventable) health risks. And the international scientific community recently stressed that robust environmental risk assessments cannot be optional.

Ultimately, Europe should widen and accelerate its access to pesticide-free alternatives. It must also support farmers in their efforts to transition away from pesticides, towards a more sustainable and resilient model.

So, what can be done? First, the EU must close the tap on pesticide use and production, and support farmers transitioning to safer alternatives. Second, it’s time for leaders to hold Big Polluters accountable for the damage they cause – not force the bill onto regular taxpayers and families harmed by these toxic substances.

Florence, Franck, and Isabelle’s children are among the hundreds of thousands already affected by pesticides. And they show that victims of pesticides are not just a statistic.

The ‘Food and Feed Safety Omnibus’ raises fundamental questions. Who exactly is the EU’s food policy supposed to protect? How many more children need to be harmed for politicians to act? And what kind of future do EU institutions want to build? 

Should pesticide protections be treated as obstacles to short-term profits, or should children be able to grow up safely? 

Politicians should reject this devastating Omnibus proposal and work instead to support the EU’s transition to safe, sustainable, and resilient farming.

Instead, the employment agency that arranged her job had quietly enrolled her in school.

She discovered this only after translating the papers she had been given. One said she was a student at an adult secondary school in Sieradz, another enrolled her at a Polish university. But Maria had never applied to either institution, attended a class or even heard of them.

Her case is part of a wider trade in fake student documents that exploited Poland’s labour and immigration systems. Employment agencies used fictitious student status to make foreign workers cheaper to employ, while private universities issued certificates that could help foreigners obtain visas or legalise their stay.

An investigation by the Polish publication Onet found the same schools and universities repeatedly appearing in documents issued to foreign workers from around the world. Some institutions existed largely on paper; in other cases, fraudsters forged documents in the names of legitimate schools without their knowledge.

The schemes went beyond fake student cards. Private universities also issued certificates used to obtain visas, enter the Schengen area or legalise residency.

They cost Poland’s social-security system millions of zloty and left some migrants facing job losses, residency problems and possible deportation – while people linked to the schools have established ties to Poland’s pro-Russian organisations and media.

Read more

EU’s new cross‑border work rules favour recruitment, not workers, say critics

Fake students cheaper for employers

Polish labour laws incentivise employment of students aged up to 26 under so-called agreements to perform a job. It means employers do not have to pay social security or health insurance contributions for them. The workers cost less than regular employees.

So, student status has become a sought-after commodity that employment agencies have exploited for gains.

A central figure in the case is Dariusz M., a school head in Sieradz detained by police in late May. When reporters from TVN24 posed as employers looking for a way to legalise the employment of foreign immigrants, M. offered to enrol them as students for 750 zloty (around €175) per person.

Prosecutors suspect him of participating in an organised group that allegedly issued around 2,500 false study certificates, costing the Polish state nearly six million zloty (more than €1.4m) in unpaid contributions.

Documents were often arranged by employment agencies with foreign workers unaware they had formally been enrolled at a school.

“In most cases, they do not even know they are involved in something illegal. They trust the employment agency,” said Rocio Flores, president of the Union of Latin American Workers in Poland.

When an inspection uncovers the fraud, the foreign workers face losing their jobs, residency problems and, in some cases, deportation. “We migrants suffer most as a result,” Flores said.

Inspections carried out by Poland’s social insurance authority confirmed there were many such cases.

In August, Dziennik Gazeta Prawna reported that Poland’s social insurance body (ZUS) stepped up inspections of companies employing foreigners with pupil or student status.

They reported that inspectors uncovered cases in which agencies pay schools for fake study certificates despite the worker having never attended classes, with Poland’s social welfare system losing out on millions of zloty.

Schools oblivious to study scam

Not all paperwork for fake students came from education institutions themselves. Some student cards and study certificates were forged in the name of real schools without their knowledge, as was the case of a Cosinus network branch in the town of Piaseczno.

Its head, Elżbieta Gotchold-Leśniewski, showed Onet reporters a file containing 62 forgeries found in various parts of Poland and had been issued to people from South America, Africa, Asia and Europe. “That is not my signature, and the school’s hologram is wrong too. In fact, many things are wrong,” she said.

Read more

Von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech risks making border pushbacks ‘normal’ EU migration policy

The forgers incorrectly copied the four-leaf clover in the school’s logo, giving rise to the term “fake four-leaf clovers” in the Polish website’s headline. The documents were nevertheless convincing enough to be accepted by employers or used by holders during ticket inspections on public transport.

A student card and certificate package cost 200 to 800 zloty (€45 to €180). One man called the school directly because he had paid 600 (€140) zloty for a set of documents and wanted to know when classes would begin. The school’s staff told him he was, in fact, not registered there at all.

Dodgy paperwork for 20+ nationalities

Since 2022, Poland’s border guard has been investigating a group that, under the cover of three private universities, sold foreigners documents needed to obtain visas or legalise their stays.

]]> AI chatbots turn users’ most intimate data into a potential goldmine for advertisers, researchers warn https://euobserver.com/239963/ai-chatbots-turn-users-most-intimate-data-into-a-potential-goldmine-for-advertisers-researchers-warn/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 06:51:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=239963 Researchers found that even when users rejected non-essential cookies, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Gemini, Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude still connected to Google Ads.]]> Six out of nine of the most popular AI chatbots routinely exposed user input to third parties, new European research reveals.

Multiple chatbots disclosed sensitive user data to advertising companies through trackers – a piece of code used to identify and target users on the web with customised advertisements, which are widely used across the web.

And tech companies may have been able to link conversation summaries with personal identifiers, allowing users to be targeted based on their conversations with AI.

The researchers aimed to establish the connection between existing tracking technologies and AI advertising. “We basically connected the dots, and wanted to test whether and how AI bots integrate tracking and advertising services,” said Narseo Vallina-Rodriguez, who led the study.

Vallina-Rodriguez is part of a group of researchers who investigated the use of ad trackers in the most popular AI providers with colleagues at Imdea, a public research institute in Madrid.

Their findings warn of “tensions” between tech company practices and obligations to users under privacy laws.

Sensitive user-data shared 

“We already knew that tracking is pervasive, even without AI. But now you have the most super-invasive phenomena on the internet, which is AI,” said Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, a policy adviser at digital rights group Edri.

Users often share information about their health, psychological state, finances, and other intimate matters in AI prompts. The study shows how users who asked AI questions about such matters could have sensitive details summarised in a chat title shared with third parties. 

“Now, big tech has access to much more intimate information which users tell AI. It’s crazy, the details are so intimate. My friends ask AI bots about relationships, or they use ‘doctor AI’,” said Domínguez de Olazábal.

GDPR rules require companies to make clear how users’ data is harvested, but researchers question “ambiguous expressions” used to explain the role of trackers in T&Cs.

And the ePrivacy directive requires users to consent to cookies unless they are “strictly necessary”, but researchers found that even when users rejected non-essential cookies, AI bots Perplexity, DeepSeek, Gemini, Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude still connected to Google Ads.

All of the top nine most popular chatbots were found to integrate at least one third-party advertising or tracking service.

Read more

EU data chief adds voice to unions’ fears of ‘carte blanche’ use of workers’ data for AI

Consent and transparency ‘shortcomings’

A preview of the study, released in May, prompted the Spanish privacy watchdog AEPD to request for the European Data Protection Committee (EPDC) to share preliminary findings with European counterparts “for knowledge and assessment”.

The final paper, titled ‘Prompt like a Butterfly, Sting like a Tracker’, has been accepted for publication at an academic forum in Delft next year.

Findings “highlight tensions between current practices and obligations under the GDPR and ePrivacy Directive, exposing broader shortcomings in consent, access control, and transparency mechanisms,” the paper reads.

It reveals that Grok, operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI, exposed public links to conversations by default, allowing trackers to routinely access whole conversations, with TikTok also processing screenshots of Grok conversations.

Read more

Grok scandal prompts MEP move to ban non-consensual AI porn in new omnibus

Meanwhile, Mistral, France’s flagship AI firm, did not offer users a choice to reject non-essential cookies. 

But offering such a choice might soon be redundant anyway. “The tracking industry is moving towards paradigms called cookie-less and identity-based tracking. So they are circumventing anti-tracking capabilities,” Vallina-Rodriguez told EUobserver.

One way, or another …

Some suggest that using browsers with anti-tracker technologies can help users avoid surveillance.

    Hundreds of people were still camping yesterday at Puerta del Sol in Madrid. They were demanding action on housing, as rents and property prices continue to rise.

    Following an outcry triggered by the eviction of an 83-year-old woman from her home, and the mobilization of thousands of people across Spain, the government adopted two housing decrees.

    Read more

    EU moves to curb Airbnb‑style rentals in bid to ease housing stress

    Did they take the protesters’ demands into account?

    MariCarmen Abascal had lived in her apartment since the 1950s, having inherited the lease from her parents. But the property was bought by an investment fund, which then challenged the validity of her lease and quadrupled her rent.

    Last week, MariCarmen was evicted from her home. The eviction sparked widespread outrage and led hundreds of protesters to camp in central Madrid, calling for action.

    Yesterday, she was finally allowed to return home after reaching an agreement with the owners.

    Aside from MariCarmen’s case, the demonstrations are largely driven by young people who are fed up with rising rents and property prices, especially in major cities such as Madrid and Barcelona.

    In Madrid, property prices have risen by around 87 percent over the past ten years. That’s less than in Portugal or the Netherlands, where prices have increased even more. But it’s still a significant rise, especially as wages have grown much more slowly over the same period.

    Read more

    [Interview] ‘Poor but sexy’ Berlin faces worsening housing crisis and bad fixes, warns German economist

    Rents are taking up a huge share of people’s incomes. In Madrid, they account for almost half of tenants’ net income on average. So, how did the Spanish government respond?

    Yesterday, it adopted two housing decree-laws. The first decree would suspend evictions until 2030 and automatically extend existing rental contracts by two years.

    It would also introduce tighter rules on seasonal rentals and prevent speculative investment funds from acquiring housing until 2028.

    The second decree is more ambitious. It would allow tenants to extend their future rental contracts indefinitely. This is what the tenants’ union has been calling for.

    Landlords would no longer be able to end a lease simply because it had reached its expiry date. Tenants who pay their rent and respect their legal obligations could remain in their homes for as long as they wish.

    This would also limit rent increases, since rents can only be raised moderately during an existing contract.

    So, the government has taken the protesters’ demands into account. But there is still a major obstacle: as our Spanish partner El Salto reports, the tenants’ union fears that this second measure may not pass through Parliament.

    That could explain why the government adopted two separate decrees. The first is considered easier to get through Parliament.

    Now, what about the EU’s proposals to tackle rising rents? We discussed them earlier this month.

    Read more

    Listen: Can the EU really make housing more affordable?

    One of the main proposals concerns short-term rentals. The idea is to introduce restrictions, particularly in tourist areas where housing is under strong pressure. By bringing more homes back onto the long-term rental market, the Commission hopes to ease pressure on prices.

    But these proposals have not yet been adopted, so we’ll have to wait and see what impact they have. And in any case, more will need to be done at national level.

    Even if prices stop rising, they are already so high that many workers can no longer afford to live in major cities.

    More social housing is needed, as well as more renovation. Increasing the supply of decent, affordable homes could help ease pressure on rents and property prices.

    ]]>         Divided EU cyber defence faces real-life Russian and Chinese threats https://euobserver.com/240301/divided-eu-cyber-defence-faces-real-life-russian-and-chinese-threats/ Wed, 30 Sep 2026 08:32:13 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240301 From phishing attacks on Polish soldiers to near-blackouts in winter, the EU’s fragmented cyber defence is seeing Russian online threats spill into real‑world dangers for ordinary Europeans. ]]> Europe is facing more immediate cyber threats, but whether its member states are prepared to deal with it collectively is becoming a question harder to answer.

    Even as drone threats, such as Russia’s bomb plot at the Leipzig-Halle airport in Germany in August, dominated European headlines in September, other, less visible hybrid attacks are also being waged against the EU every day, whose sheer weight of numbers should also cause grave concern.

    Poland, for instance, recorded 4,200 cyber-security incidents in military networks and systems in 2024 and 7,100 in 2025, Polish cyber command spokesperson, Przemek Lipczyński, told EUobserver.

    In 2025, Polish security systems blocked four million phishing emails targeted at soldiers and defence personnel.

    And Poland aside, evolving technology meant Russian cyber-attacks “do not know any border”, said Jamila Boutemeur, the EU’s head of cybersecurity body, in what amounted to a single market for hacking.

    For its part, the European Union has built its cybersecurity architecture around the Boutemeur’s European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, ENISA, in Athens, as well as the 27 national cybersecurity agencies.

    But as Russia’s threat levels up, the European structure is seeing familiar problems: information is not always shared, responsibilities remain divided between national governments and EU institutions, while ENISA itself is being asked to do more with limited resources.

    And the European Court of Auditors (ECA) confirmed it on 21 September in its ENISA study.

    “The architecture is there, the structure is there. Now it’s a matter of willingness and trust,” to effectively fight back, said George-Marius Hyzler, the ECA’s main auditor.

    Stress test shows EU cracks

    “It always boils down to the same thing, lack of information sharing,” he said, identifying the EU’s key weakness.

    Read more

    Auditors find EU cyber‑attack response is weakened by overlapping systems and secretive member states

    And for Czech Greens MEP Markéta Gregorová, who is also the lead rapporteur on the EU’s incoming Cybersecurity Act 2 (CSA2), duplication of work also bedevilled the EU’s response.

    “The [ECA] auditors describe a system that does not work” and was “wasteful”, she told EUobserver.

    “Six European legal acts force the same company to report the same incident to different authorities. Two EU bodies monitor the same threats,” Gregorová said.

    She also advocated a stronger operational role for ENISA.

    But the EU fault lines have underlying political as well as legal tensions.

    Cybersecurity remains largely within the competence of the member states, and governments differ in how much new power they are willing to delegate to European institutions.

    And for Dimitar Lilkov, from the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies, there were three main sources of friction: national security, trust, and money.

    ]]>         EU states urged to ‘go beyond’ AI Act to protect people from abusive surveillance https://euobserver.com/240371/eu-states-urged-to-go-beyond-ai-act-to-protect-people-from-abusive-surveillance/ Wed, 30 Sep 2026 04:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240371 Peaceful protesters and ethnic minorities in Europe could be victimised by police abuse of AI-powered surveillance tech, an EU rights body has warned. ]]> As AI-powered biometric identification is adopted by police, national authorities should go beyond legal requirements to build trust within the public, a watchdog report has advised.

    “To build public trust, law enforcement should publish the results of their fundamental rights impact assessments, going beyond what the AI Act requires,” said the Fundamental Rights Agency (FRA), an EU branch which keeps tabs on citizens’ freedoms, in Vienna on Wednesday (30 September).

    After collecting data from seven EU countries (France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Italy, the Netherlands, and Ireland), the watchdog warned that several member states have yet to put necessary frameworks in place as they adopt automated systems to identify people.

    Remote biometric identification is increasingly used to compare people’s profiles against databases or watch lists, but as the technology develops it could be rolled out for real-time use in public areas. 

    “With clear safeguards and independent oversight, remote biometric technologies can support policing without undermining the very freedoms it is meant to safeguard. Ultimately, it is about trust,” said FRA chief Sirpa Rautio.

    Read more

    [Interview] EU rights chief: ‘Governments don’t want to be scrutinised’

    Call for disclosure mechanisms 

    Effective implementation of the EU AI Act requires clear national laws and consistent safeguards to ensure that AI-powered technologies are not used to identify people taking part in peaceful demonstrations or public gatherings, the FRA says.

    The body warns that automated identification of live data may affect people’s private lives and interfere with their right to protection of personal data.

    In its survey, 37 percent of people said they fear their data could be used for unauthorised purposes. 

    And 29 percent of people surveyed by FRA said they would be less willing to take part in peaceful demonstrations or protests if facial recognition was used.

    The FRA is worried that surveillance tech powered by AI could be used in exactly those scenarios.

    In principle, the EU’s AI Act adopted in 2024 bans real-time remote biometric identification systems in public spaces. But exemptions exist for law enforcement authorities using the technology for finding victims or missing persons, to prevent threats to life or physical safety, stop a terror attack, or to find criminal suspects.

    ]]>         Frugal EU states seeking budget cuts are shooting their own regions in the foot https://euobserver.com/240275/eu-states-seeking-budget-cuts-are-shooting-their-own-regions-in-the-foot/ Tue, 29 Sep 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240275 Despite joining a frugal ultimatum for EU budget cuts, the Dutch get roughly as much growth from EU investment as they pay in, while narrowing the gap between wealthier and poorer regions.]]> Six frugal countries this week circulated a letter threatening to block a deal on the next EU budget unless “hundreds of billions” of euros in spending was cut. 

    The Dutch and Germans, ever the most zealous keepers of the frugal flame, want to redirect what remains away from regional and farming funds, towards innovation and defence.  

    For those following EU fiscal debates, this song will sound familiar. So-called ‘net payer’ countries have never liked sending money to the economic periphery. 

    In 2013, after a year of bickering, Britain, Germany, and the Netherlands killed a European Commission plan for a five percent increase and pushed through the EU’s first-ever budget cut, with farm and cohesion funds taking the biggest hit.

    But new research suggests that the frugals may be shooting themselves in the foot. 

    Last week, Olga Ivanova, a senior researcher at the Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency (PBL), published a study in Dutch economics journal ESB calculating what EU money actually does for the Netherlands’ 12 provinces. 

    And, for most of them, she found that the growth effect of EU investment outweighed their share of what the Netherlands paid into the budget. 

    Using PBL’s own economic model, she traced 10 EU funding streams between 2013 and 2024, from Horizon science research grants to farm subsidies and regional development money. 

    Across the Netherlands as a whole, provinces get back about 99 cents in extra growth for every euro paid out to the EU budget.

      <description><p>Fears that US deficit is unsustainable also drive UK 30-year bond yields briefly above 6% for first time since 1998</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/oct/01/uk-house-prices-september-mortgage-rates-bonds-stock-markets-manufacturing-latest-news-updates">Business live – latest updates</a></p></li></ul><p>The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading.</p><p>The threat of a renewed round of inflation from <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/24/global-bond-sell-off-pressures-uk-borrowing-costs-budget">the persistently high cost of oil</a> has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/01/global-bond-sell-off-uk-long-term-borrowing-costs-us-bond-yield">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Trump criticized $2.4bn rehab amid attempts to pressure then Fed chair Jerome Powell into lowering interest rates</p><p>An internal watchdog said the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released on Wednesday.</p><p>For over a year, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a> has centered his attacks against the Fed and former chair <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/jerome-powell">Jerome Powell</a> around the renovations, including a months-long Department of Justice criminal investigation that was <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/apr/24/doj-drops-criminal-probe-jerome-powell-fed">dropped</a> in April.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/federal-reserve-watchdog-building-renovation">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/inflation-report-interest-rates-fed</link>
      <description><p>Traders see about a 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from ​about 45% following White House pressure</p><p>Good economic news boosted Wall Street’s main indexes on Wednesday, as a softer-than-anticipated <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/inflation">inflation</a> reading buoyed up hopes that the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> might not hike rates as soon ⁠as next month.</p><p>A commerce department report ⁠showed the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) ​price index stood at 3.4% on an annual basis in August against estimates of 3.7%, per economists polled by Reuters.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/inflation-report-interest-rates-fed">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>A ‘freaked out’ US food industry is hitting back at Maha – with social media influencers</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/us-food-industry-maga-social-media-influencers</link>
      <description><p>Cross-partisan support in Washington on issues like pesticides and food additives pose a threat to the industry’s bottom line </p><p>Some of the biggest food and agriculture corporations in the US are funding a campaign that pays social media influencers to combat elements of Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again platform, according to an investigation by the Guardian and Documented, an investigative watchdog and journalism project.</p><p>The ascension of RFK Jr to secretary of health and human services has boosted his putative campaign to end chronic illness in the US, which he believes is primarily caused by processed foods and dyes, exposure to certain chemicals, and poor farming practices, along with an overuse of what he falsely claims are dangerous vaccines. The “Maha” movement blends long-running mainstream concerns about food and farm safety with conspiracy theories about everything from medicine to milk. A Maha “<a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/28/vance-rfk-tyson-hines-maha-summit-01095218">summit</a>” in Washington this week will feature JD Vance and several members of Trump’s cabinet.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/30/us-food-industry-maga-social-media-influencers">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>It marks another ratcheting up of Trump’s trade war and affects nearly $1bn in imports of a $880bn trade relationship</p><p>US-<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/canada">Canada</a> relations, already tense, are likely to deteriorate further after the United States went ahead early on Tuesday with a decision to ban nearly $1bn worth of Canadian imports, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles.</p><p>The ban amounts to barely a ripple in $880bn worth of annual two-way trade between the two northern neighbors.       <title>As the US midterms approach, Trump’s boasts on the economy fall flat with voters</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/28/trump-us-economy-midterm-elections</link>
      <description><p>Trump’s tariffs and his war against Iran caused prices to rise, but the US president continues to claim it’s ‘the greatest economy in history’</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/04/sign-up-to-the-stakes-2026-your-weekly-guide-to-the-us-midterms">Sign up for The Stakes 2026: your weekly guide to the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>Donald Trump has taken to repeating a familiar boast: “<a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/pool-reports-september-16-2026">We have the greatest economy</a> in history,” Trump said recently at a White House press gaggle. The boast comes even though inflation is higher and economic growth lower than when Joe Biden left office, even though <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/business/energy/gas-prices-trump-midterms-iran-rcna598523">gas prices have jumped about 50%</a> since the war against Iran started, and even though <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/15/polls/times-siena-poll-likely-voter-crosstabs.html">73% of Americans think the economy</a> is in fair or poor shape (48% say it’s in poor shape). What’s more, the Federal Reserve is so worried about inflation that it just raised interest rates.</p><p>“It’s bluster, it’s gaslighting for him to say the economy is the greatest ever,” said Darrick Hamilton, chief economist for the AFL-CIO, the nation’s main union federation. “The economy is trending down by many measures. A lot of that has been caused by Trump’s unforced errors.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/28/trump-us-economy-midterm-elections">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>On the rocks? Scotch distilleries pause production as unsold ‘whisky loch’ grows</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/sep/29/scotch-distilleries-pause-production-whisky-loch-scotland</link>
      <description><p>Demand for Scotland’s most famous export has slumped, with industry facing job cuts and closures</p><p>Obscured by the Scottish countryside on the outskirts of Kirkcaldy, Cluny bond is, in effect, a small town built to store whisky. By the time the latest set of warehouses are finished on the former opencast coal mine, Diageo’s 220-hectare (544-acre) maturation campus will be able to store almost 3m casks of Scotch. The drinks multinational needs the space.</p><p>After a 15-year boom turbocharged by the Covid-19 pandemic, demand for Scotch whisky has slumped around the world. Distilleries have paused production across Scotland to avoid adding to the glut of supply, known as a “whisky loch” – the equivalent of a “wine lake”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/sep/29/scotch-distilleries-pause-production-whisky-loch-scotland">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/ng-interactive/2026/sep/27/democracy-ai-datacenters-power</link>
      <description><p>‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’</p><p>The Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/silicon-valley">Silicon Valley</a> mogul to discuss what a state designed to maximize science and tech powered by commercial models might look like. The gathered technologists were drawn to the idea of building a small nation-state dedicated to the endeavor, Reich recalls in “<a href="https://systemerrorbook.com">System Error</a>: Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot it”.</p><p>When Reich asked whether this state would be a democracy, he got a cool no. “Democracy is too slow, and it holds science back,” he was told. “To optimize for science, we need a beneficent technocrat in charge.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/ng-interactive/2026/sep/27/democracy-ai-datacenters-power">Continue reading...</a></description>
