— Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) September 28, 2026

Wierusz-Kowalski, who was active in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, was a renowned realist painter whose work often featured animals alongside people. His Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow had, by the 1930s, become part of the collection of Andrzej Rotwand, a wealthy banker and industrialist.

In June 1939, it was featured in an exhibition organised by the Society for the Encouragement of Fine Arts in Warsaw, which occupied the building that is now the famous Zachęta National Gallery of Art.

However, the exhibition was brought to an abrupt end when Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. The works on display, along with other items from the gallery, were seized by the occupiers, with many used to decorate the offices and apartments of German officials.

Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow was displayed in a club for high-ranking SS and police officers located in Warsaw’s Blanka Palace. The same building also housed Warsaw’s German-installed commissioner, Helmut Otto, and mayor, Ludwig Leist.

 

No information has been released as to the fate of the painting in the immediate aftermath of the war. However, it eventually came into the possession of Ewa Tsonis, who has now handed it back.

Speaking at a ceremony in the National Museum in Warsaw, Tsonis said that her late father, Michał Stefan Koryzna, had purchased the painting in the 1960s from Desa, a major gallery and auction house, in the city of Kraków.

“I grew up with this painting. It was greatly appreciated and loved in our family,” she said. However, after recently conducting research into the painting’s history, she became aware of its provenance and notified the culture ministry.

Ewa Tsonis (right) alongside the painting with culture minister Marta Cienkowska (centre) and the director of the national museum in Warsaw, Agnieszka Lajus

Experts from the National Museum in Warsaw confirmed the identity of the painting, which remains in good condition and in its original frame. Tsonis then donated the work to the museum.

“Restitution is not possible without the cooperation of many people and institutions – both on the side of the state and on the part of the owners of the works,” said Cienkowska, who thanked Tsonis for her “incredibly responsible and civic-minded attitude”.

“Such attitudes are still rare but, because we constantly talk about restitution – we search for lost works and strive to recover them – we are increasingly approached by people who own lost objects and feel a sense of responsibility for cultural heritage.”

Cienkowska noted that the culture ministry has so far secured the return of over 920 works, with around 200 more restitution cases currently underway in 18 countries.

Germany has agreed to return to Poland a collection of 73 medieval documents that were looted during WWII.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 1, 2025

However, that is still just a small fraction of the over 60,000 missing items listed in the ministry’s database of missing works, which includes seven further paintings by Wierusz-Kowalski.

Two other works from Rotwand’s collection – Italian Woman by Anna Bilińska and Mother with Children by Kazimierz Alchimowicz – were also hung in the SS officers’ club during the war and today remain missing.

Poland has in recent years stepped up efforts to secure the return of historical and cultural items looted during the German and Soviet occupations.

In 2022, it appealed to UNESCO for help in securing the return of cultural items that remain missing after being looted by Nazi Germany. It also launched a campaign seeking the return of thousands of items that ended up in Russia after the war.

Poland is changing the procedures under which its military can fire upon foreign aircraft, citing the “growing threat from Russia”. Visual identification of targets will no longer be required, with other forms of data to be used instead.

The move follows a series of violations of Polish airspace over the last year by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter, as well as Russia’s increasing use of jet-powered drones to attack targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border.

“In the coming days, the defence minister will change the procedures for firing by Polish planes and helicopters at objects flying to us from the direction of Russia,” announced deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk on Monday, quoted by news service Defence24.

The change, as Tomczyk explained in a statement later issued on social media, will shift requirements away from requiring visual identification of foreign aerial objects and towards so-called “positive identification”.

The latter involves identifying an object based on a combination of several other, non-visual sources of information, such as using radar and other sensors to determine its speed, altitude, trajectory and flight parameters, as well as a lack of IFF (identification friend or foe) from an object.

 

Tomczyk said that the change was being made based on the “conclusions from recent weeks” made by the operational commander of Poland’s armed forces, General Ireneusz Nowak.

It is a “response to the growing threat from Russia, experiences from the war in Ukraine, and the emergence of new air attack means – primarily fast jet drones and cruise missiles in the case of which the time for reaction is very brief”, added Tomczyk.

He noted that accurate target identification is particularly crucial in peacetime, when there are civilian aircraft in Polish airspace.

Several early medieval Arabic silver coins have been found in a forest near Elbląg in northern Poland. Experts believe they may have belonged to merchants travelling to or from the Viking Age port of Truso, which was situated nearby.

The silver dirhams date back around 1,200 years, to the first half of the ninth century, before the founding of the Polish state. They may have remained in circulation until the turn of the 10th/11th century, the time of the settlement’s collapse.

The discovery of the “new treasure” was announced last week by the Archaeological and Historical Museum in Elbląg. It did not reveal who had unearthed them, but said that the find had taken place during a legal search in a forest near the town of Młynary, just east of Elbląg.

After conservation and processing work, the coins will be included in the collection of the museum, whose archaeologists will also visit the site hoping for further finds.

The museum’s Jakub Jagodziński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the find consists of “six early medieval Arabic dirhams and two fragments of these silver coins”. He said that they are provisionally dated to the first half of the 9th century, but a more precise estimate will be possible after they are processed.

 

The coins could have belonged to merchants travelling along the routes leading to or from Truso or to Prussian guards who later collected tolls on these routes, Jagodziński explained.

Truso was a Viking Age port of trade set up by the Scandinavians on the shores of lake Druzno near the Vistula river delta. Established by the late 7th century and active until the early 11th century, its location enabled trade extending towards Kyivan Rus, Byzantium and the Islamic world.

Historians knew of Truso’s existence because of the account of the Anglo-Saxon traveller Wulfstan of Hedeby. Centuries-long efforts to find the precise site proved fruitless until it was finally discovered in the early 1980s by the young archaeologist Marek Jagodziński, Jakub’s father.

Finds of Arab coins in Poland are not unprecedented. A silver deposit was discovered in 1986 on the site of Truso itself, consisting of 11 complete coins and five fragments. Coins found there were minted in places including Baghdad and Damascus, according to the Medievalists.net website.

More recently, in 2024, a fragment of an early medieval Arabic dirham was found during renovations of an old manor house on the Baltic coast in northwestern Poland.

In transactions involving dirhams, it was the value of the silver that mattered, so the coins were often broken into pieces, archaeologist Grzegorz Kurka told PAP.

“Therefore, when hoards of Arab coins are discovered in Poland, they are divided into several pieces. Whole coins are also found, but much less frequently,” he explained.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Fri, 02 Oct 2026 08:40:19 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.6 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Aldi debt jumps by £100m as profit slips at discount grocer https://www.cityam.com/aldi-debt-jumps-by-100m-as-profit-slips-at-discount-grocer/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 08:40:05 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2462650

Aldi took on more than £100m in net debt last year, as the discount grocer’s profit slipped despite its blockbuster expansion plans.  The supermarket chain, the UK’s fourth largest, saw its net debt grow by a fifth in 2025, from £717m to £862m.  Aldi’s jump in debt comes despite the grocer’s plans to expand rapidly [...]]]>

Aldi took on more than £100m in net debt last year, as the discount grocer’s profit slipped despite its blockbuster expansion plans. 

The supermarket chain, the UK’s fourth largest, saw its net debt grow by a fifth in 2025, from £717m to £862m. 

Aldi’s jump in debt comes despite the grocer’s plans to expand rapidly in the UK. Last week, chief executive Giles Hurley announced £900m in funding to open 40 new stores next year.

Hurley said last week that the supermarket’s operating profit held steady at £433m last year, though new company filings show its pre-tax profit slipped from £416m to £400m.

The family-owned grocer’s workforce fell from 50,655 to 49,661 in the year to December 2025, its filings revealed, suggesting it cut about 1,000 staff in the year. 

Despite the falling headcount, the supermarket chain’s wage costs jumped from £1.43bn to £1.46bn.

Aldi eyes more market share

Aldi’s debt pile, while rising, remains well below that of some of its private-equity-owned rivals. 

Net debt at Morrisons, which is owned by New York-based Clayton, Dubilier & Rice, jumped from £7.1bn to £7.5bn in the year to October. Asda, owned by London-based TDR Capital, has debts of £3.5bn. 

While Asda and Morrisons have sought to sell off the freehold rights to some of its shops in a bid to push down their debt piles, Aldi is hoping to put more pressure on the UK’s ‘big four’ supermarkets. 

Aldi and fellow German discounter Lidl have surged to dominance of Britain’s grocery market in recent decades. Morrisons is now the UK’s fifth-biggest supermarket, having been leapfrogged by Aldi earlier this year.

Aldi is within one per cent of Asda’s market share, though its control of the market has weakened from 10.8 to 10.6 per cent over the past year, according to figures from Worldpanel. 

Announcing the grocer’s results last week, Hurley hit out at rival supermarkets for offering loyalty discounts, which he says give shoppers a misleading impression of value.

He told reporters: “One of the drivers of their growth is the fact that their retail prices are going up, and some of them are seeing volume decline at the same time.

“We are driving prices down, and we’re growing our volumes, and that is hugely important in continuing to reinforce our confidence around growing our business and expanding.”

Aldi UK is part of the grocery chain’s Aldi Sud branch, which is controlled by the heirs of Karl Albrecht. He co-founded the grocer with his brother, Theo, in 1946.

Aldi was contacted for comment.

IG’s shares plunged in early morning trading on Friday after it was forced to cut its annual revenue forecast.

The spread betting company saw its share drop 26 per cent to 950p per share. Shares are down 23.7 per cent since January.

The sharp fall follows the group’s revenue falling 14 per cent year on year during the third quarter after it retained less of its customer’s trading activity as revenue on over the counter trading (OTC) business.

OTC trading is where customers can trade assets without using a primary stock exchange.

OTC revenue retention slid to 70 per cent from 80 per cent, which the FTSE 100 group has averaged since its introduction in the second half of 2025.

The online trading platform now expects full year revenue growth to be in “a mid-single-digit per cent range” year on year.

The platform had previously expected revenue to increase between 10 and 15 per cent on an organic basis, after hiking its performance outlook in May.

Market conditions

Earnings before tax are anticipated to be in the “low-40s per cent range” for the financial year, a decline from last period’s 47 per cent.

Chief executive Breon Corcoran blamed the decline on “less supportive market conditions”, as despite the fall in revenue customer demand remained robust.

Organic first trades rose more than 25 per cent, while active customer numbers climbed 17 per cent.

Income generated from OTC customers also grew eight per cent.

The investing platform’s acquisition Underdog, a sports prediction market, also saw net revenue more than double to $105m, ahead of its “seasonally important” fourth quarter.

But the Board expects to meet its medium-term guidance beyond 2026, anticipating further customer growth off the back of continued investment into products coupled with “higher OTC revenue retention.

City AM understands that Fahnbulleh is in direct contact with US energy secretary Chris Wright to discuss a US move to potentially choke off [...]]]>

Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is holding crunch talks with her American counterpart about an escalating diesel spat that has seen Treasury secretary Scott Bessent urge Europe to release emergency reserves “immediately”.

City AM understands that Fahnbulleh is in direct contact with US energy secretary Chris Wright to discuss a US move to potentially choke off diesel exports to Europe that threatens to upend supply and send prices at the pump soaring, a person familiar with the discussions said.

The UK and Europe are being pressured by the Trump administration to tap into their emergency stockpiles of the fuel to relieve a major global shortage sparked by the conflict in the Middle East.

The President is weighing a range of protectionist trade measures should Europe refuse to release its reserves, ranging from curbing exports to select countries to an all out ban on US-produced diesel.

On Wednesday, Bessent ramped up pressure on European allies, telling them to tap into their stockpiles “immediately” and “match… their commitments with action”. In a post on social media, he wrote: “Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.”

He added that American truck drivers, farmers and businesses “should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel fuel shortage”.

Europe has been racing to agree a joint response to the US’s pressure, which comes just weeks before the country’s pivotal mid-term elections in which prices at the pump have become a major talking point.

Energy minister Martin McCluskey joined a call with EU commissioners on Thursday to weigh their response, a person familliar with discussions said. But participants could not commit any concrete actions beyond agreeing “to maintain close contact” as events develop.

America’s broadsides are believed to be aimed predominantly at France and Germany, which have access to a considerably larger pool of emergency reserves than the UK.

Diesel prices ‘extreme’ – Healey

But any loss of US diesel would be enormously damaging for Britain, which currently imports over half its supply of the refined fuel. Roughly a third of that currently comes from the States, meaning any ban would choke off one of the country’s major sources of supply in an already starved global market.

Adding to the situation’s severity is the prospect of Britain’s largest refinery shuttering its operations for 10 weeks as for planned maintenance. The Fawley site in Hampshire is responsible for producing kerosene for Heathrow and a fifth of diesel used at British forecourts.

Diesel prices have been rising across the globe, as some of the world’s largest refineries became targets in both the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts. In Britain, the fuel has climbed to 200p a litre, nearing the record set during the height of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

For drivers, the rise means it costs almost £110 to fill up a typical family car, £31 more than before the onset of the Iran war.

Chancellor John Healey acknowledged diesel prices were “extreme” in an interview at Labour party conference.

“In the end, we’re also working with the Americans where we can try and put in place what will solve this, or at least significantly ease it,” he said, “which would be a diplomatic settlement [and] an end to the fighting with Iran.”

A spoksewoman for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”

]]> 2462479Ali Lyon Ali Lyon Wetherspoon boss attacks Labour for ‘high street dereliction’ as profit falls https://www.cityam.com/wetherspoon-scathes-labour-for-high-street-dereliction-as-profit-falls/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 06:25:11 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2462614

Pub chain Wetherspoon has hit out at the government for causing “high street dereliction” by hiking taxes, as the company’s profit slipped by a quarter.  The London-listed pub group saw revenue jump by five per cent to £2.2bn in the year to July – in line with analyst forecasts – though pre-tax profit fell further [...]]]>

Pub chain Wetherspoon has hit out at the government for causing “high street dereliction” by hiking taxes, as the company’s profit slipped by a quarter. 

The London-listed pub group saw revenue jump by five per cent to £2.2bn in the year to July – in line with analyst forecasts – though pre-tax profit fell further than expected, by 28 per cent to £59m. 

Sir Tim Martin, Wetherspoon’s chairman, blamed the Labour government for hiking business rates, minimum wages and national insurance contributions (NICs). 

He said: “The hospitality industry, as many commentators and companies have noted, has borne the brunt of government-led tax and regulatory cost increases, especially in the last two budgets. 

“This has resulted in pubs becoming even more expensive than supermarkets, leading to job losses, closures and high street dereliction.”

Wetherspoon is famed for its rock-bottom prices, but analysts have predicted that this could mean rising taxes and energy costs will weigh more heavily on it than some of its higher-margin rivals.  The pubco’s operating margin slimmed from 6.9 to 5.4 per cent in the last year. 

Heatwaves boost summer sales

The FTSE 250 pub firm blamed a five per cent increase in costs for its falling profit. The group paid £46 more in wages, £31m more in repairs and £9m more in business rates last year.

Wetherspoon’s energy costs jumped by 77 per cent to £40m last year, it told shareholders. Energy costs and packaging taxes have also “weighed heavily” on hospitality firms in recent years, Martin said. 

The pub firm said its sales picked up in recent months, helped by “exceptional weather”. Like-for-like sales grew by 8.6 per cent in the last nine weeks, it said. 

This has been helped by “substantial progress in recent years in increasing the number of beer gardens and outside seating areas”. 

Martin claimed Wetherspoon is outperforming the wider pub sector. Like-for-like sales at the company grew by 7.7 per cent in August, compared to sector-wide growth of 0.8 per cent, according to NIQ figures. 

The Wetherspoon boss reiterated his calls for John Healey to cut VAT on hospitality firms from 20 to 10 per cent. 

The pub chain has backed a campaign, led by celebrity chef Tom Kerridge, which claims this tax break would be the easiest way to prevent swathes of insolvencies and job losses on the high street.

Shares in JD Wetherspoon jumped eight per cent to 880.5p in early trading.

Hit Point star Nick Blood tells us what he’d eat for his last meal on earth, from his mum’s Sunday roast to his favourite taco restaurant I was a very fussy kid. If I saw an onion in a dish, I’d be picking that out. There’s a bit of carrot, there’s a bit of celery: [...]]]>

Hit Point star Nick Blood tells us what he’d eat for his last meal on earth, from his mum’s Sunday roast to his favourite taco restaurant

I was a very fussy kid. If I saw an onion in a dish, I’d be picking that out. There’s a bit of carrot, there’s a bit of celery: get those out. My mum did most of the cooking – all the standard stuff: spag bol, lasagne, roast dinners. I loved a good roast dinner on a Sunday, it was my favourite meal of the week. My grandma and mum were brilliant at it – it was a big family occasion and the leftovers, which are the best part, went on for days.

It’s important to get the condiments right: pork and apple sauce or turkey and cranberry – and it has to have roast potatoes. Oh, and Yorkshire puddings – I’m from down south but my grandma was from Lancashire and my dad was from Liverpool, so there was a lot of northern influence in our house. I’m married to an American now and she always wants mashed potatoes but it’s got to be roast for me.

    According to the government’s estimates, satellite-reliant services alone underpin 18 per cent of UK GDP – which is perhaps not widely appreciated. A UK government which is actively engaged in the industry as a core customer would create ripple effects across the supply chain – from communications, data and analytics, to software, insurance, finance and professional services.

    The reason is that the proposed changes to the triple lock are unlikely to save much money – almost certainly not enough to cover the significant new spending on ‘free’ social care announced at the same time. That makes higher taxes inevitable – with the £18bn purported cost of the new social care service equivalent to more than a 2p in the pound increase in the base rate of income tax. 

    The speech suggested the new indexation method will be inflation or 2.5 per cent – whichever is higher – with an additional adjustment occurring to maintain a link to average wage levels over the medium term. For example, if inflation is three per cent and wage growth is four per cent in the first period, the pension will initially rise by three per cent. But if inflation then falls to two per cent while wage growth remains at four per cent in the second period, the pension will rise by five per cent to ensure it keeps pace with the cumulative eight per cent rise in wages over the full period.

    It is inconceivable that this new method can lower annual spending on pensions by £18bn by 2030. Indeed, depending on inflation and wages outcomes over the coming years, it’s possible that the changes don’t save any money at all. The public – like the bond market – should be under no illusions that this announcement will solve the UK’s economic and fiscal ills.  

    Breaking a taboo

    Although Burnham should be commended for breaking the taboo over ending the triple lock, to raise the sums needed to fund his care plans, far more radical action on pensions would be required. As Policy Exchange advocated in Beyond Our Means, one could freeze the state pension for three years and then increase it with CPI inflation, which would save around £20bn a year by 2030. Or one could means-test the state pension, as they do in my home-country of Australia.

    Alternatively, Policy Exchange has advocated funding social care by switching to a private insurance model, similar to the world-leading systems in Germany or Japan. In this model, workers would pay compulsory premiums from around age 40, with funding also supported by compulsory employee contributions for those below retirement age, and copayments, capped at a proportion of the total cost of the service. This would be a genuine market-based approach, a world away from the state-centred model of a National Care Service that appears to be envisioned.

    The plans outlined at Labour conference represent one of the largest non-crisis expansions in state-spending for decades, and a further, potentially permanent, increase in the UK’s tax burden

    This leaves only one obvious outcome: higher taxes. As a first step, the government may seek to raise this via targeted tax increases on wealth, capital gains or high-value homes – all measures that would further damage the economy and exacerbate the flight of high-tax-paying individuals from the country. But wealth taxes have a strong track record of failure, and ultimately the sums required will require a broad-based increase in taxation – paid for by ordinary workers and businesses.

    Britain is facing an energy emergency. January bills are expected to climb by £276 for the typical UK household, the largest jump in four years, and that follows the four per cent price cap increase that arrived on 1 October. 

    Burnham’s answer so far has been a VAT cut on domestic energy bills. But all this does is move money from one pocket to another, with the taxpayer covering the difference. In the meantime, not a single bottleneck in the system is addressed. 

    The real problem lies in the friction to build. UK energy costs are high because we can’t build fast enough. The private capital and appetite to build more energy generation and infrastructure exists, but grid queues, planning delays and a lack of competition are holding us back. 

    At Fuse, we have just submitted a call to action to the UK government on how to build faster, unlock growth and bring down energy bills for good. These changes are simple, entirely within the Government’s control and don’t require subsidies or public funding. 

    First, stop making projects wait up to a decade for a grid connection. Right now, if you want to build a data centre or warehouse, even with planning permission and funding it can take up to 10 years to connect to the grid, and households pay for every month of that delay. 

    The wait is so long because the grid has to offer 24/7 access to power, so projects sit in the queue until reinforcement work is finished. Instead, we must start offering developers flexible grid connections that can be switched off when congestion is at its peak. They take on that risk in exchange for a faster connection within one to two years. More projects get on the grid, fixed grid costs get spread out more widely and household bills fall. 

    Queuing behind a monopoly

    We also need to let any qualified company build grid infrastructure instead of queuing behind a monopoly. Large grid projects should go to competitive tender by default, and network operators should pay automatic compensation to connecting customers when they miss a date. All network data, including costs, timelines and forecasts should be made public. Only with this level of accountability will things actually change. 

    When it comes to planning, we must also be better at enforcing deadlines. If the statutory period expires without a decision, the application should be approved by default. If a decision arrives late, the applicant should get their fee back. Councils and agencies would treat deadlines very differently if missing one carried a cost.

    Blocking gas turbine projects is also driving up energy costs. The more renewables we add, the more we need power that runs when the sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing. Gas fills that gap. 

    Finally, we must legalise plug-in home batteries. Plug-in solar panels became legal in the UK just a few months ago, which was the right call. But the battery, the part that lets a household store their own low cost solar power for when prices spike, is still stuck behind a safety study. Germany has years of evidence from households successfully running these systems, which we should use and build on rather than start from scratch.

    Yes, the VAT cut on domestic electricity bills will offer short term relief for households this winter. But in reality it will be spent by Spring and the Treasury will have paid for a few months of lower bills with nothing to show for it. 

    The reforms above cost nothing and ministers already hold every lever they need to bring energy costs down. If they are serious about reducing bills, make it easier to build in Britain. Don’t, and we will be having the same conversation next winter with an even bigger hole in our public finances.

    Bovensiepen is the new company built around the family behind the original Alpina, and it takes its name from founder Burkard Bovensiepen. While BMW now controls the Alpina brand itself, Bovensiepen continues to modify BMWs in much the same spirit, and the latest example, based on the BMW Z4, is the Spider.

Bovensiepen has fitted an unrestricted air intake with an additional ram-air channel, a larger intake silencer and a new exhaust system designed to reduce back pressure and give the straight-six a deeper sound.     The Performance Pack adds a few more changes for buyers who want to make the most of the Spider’s extra performance. There’s an aluminium rear differential cover with larger cooling fins, an underbody V-brace to increase chassis stiffness, and the higher 183mph top speed.

The changes are relatively subtle, which suits the Bovensiepen formula, this isn’t a BMW Z4 wearing a body kit for the sake of attracting attention.     The BMW Z4 has always been a slightly unusual choice in the sports car market, and Bovensiepen’s version pushes that idea further. For buyers who remember what Alpina used to represent, that’s probably the whole appeal.

    For Manchester City 2026, see Saracens 2019. Cheating in sport is common on the pitch and it probably happens a lot more than we’d care to admit off it. But sometimes it is blatant and sometimes it is brazen.

    The independent commission’s verdict on 115 charges lodged by the Premier League against Manchester City was released on Tuesday, and it details a severe case of cheating. The club deny the claims.

    But what punishment should be bestowed on the Abi Dhabi-owned team if the guilty verdicts are upheld? For that we should look back to the biggest cheating scandal in rugby.

    Back then it was Saracens setting up companies, image rights schemes and promotional payments to skirt the salary cap. They were fined over £5m for their sins and deducted enough points – in two 35-point chunks – to relegate them. They spent a year in the second-tier Championship before coming back up.

    But was that an actual punishment? A lot of that Saracens team stayed together and, while their dominance was dented, they’ve won a title since then. Fans couldn’t even mock their existence in the Championship because the season was played behind closed doors due to the Covid-19 pandemic and the reality is they were completely fine.

    Manchester City punishment will be major

    So it begs the question: what can the Premier League and the organisation’s punishers-at-large learn from the Saracens saga? Well, don’t relegate Manchester City.

    For Saracens, the relegation, while humiliating, took them away from the spotlight. Perhaps they should have been given a points deduction every year for five years; enough to stop them reaching the top four. It would have maintained their presence within the league while punishing their wrongdoing. 

    For Manchester City, that should be the main thrust of any punishment: long-term suffering without being able to market themselves as rising from the ashes.

    But beyond that there should be other learnings from rugby. Saracens weren’t placed under a transfer ban and were able to go on as normal, so long as they remained within the salary cap.

    The Premier League should get creative with Manchester City: keep any money raised from player sales for non-league clubs in trouble; implement a complete transfer ban on players; only allow them to sign English players on loan; and ensure the punishment is visible to all who care – mainly fans.

    The point is this: I don’t believe it is in the best interests of the game to relegate Manchester City when there is a greater impact, and price to be paid, from remaining within the Premier League.

    Level playing field

    Sport is never really a level playing field and I am not sure anyone believes it ever has been. And with that, punishments should ensure that something is given back in return for all that has been taken.

    What the Premier League commission’s findings show is that brazen attempts to skirt – albeit arbitrary – footballing rules will be found out, eventually at least.

    How different organisations across sport react to that varies. The NBA’s LA Clippers were slapped with a $30m fine and their owner Steve Ballmer was banned from a year’s worth of games for paying Kawhi Leonard extra via back-door schemes.

    Yet Saracens were allowed to quietly go about their business and return without a major hit, comparatively speaking at least.

    So Manchester City is an interesting test case. And it is something the Premier League can use to deter others while ensuring that fans feel like their outrage has been heard.

    For generations of men, the tie was something you wore without thinking. Slipping one on was simply part of your morning routine, as mundane as shaving or splashing on some cologne. But then the shadow of Big Tech loomed over the corporate world, with its hoodies and its t-shirts and its trainers.

    The tie became a symbol of the old world order, something stuffy and irrelevant. Who has time to tie a double Windsor when you should be moving fast and breaking things? And then came the pandemic, with its work-from-home ethos that allowed people to Zoom into meetings wearing their pyjamas. Nobody is getting suited-up to sit at a desk in their spare room.

    I noticed this at 4am in London’s Docklands, where thousands of people were dancing in the former Guinness factory. The brutalist building, now home to the Cause, one of the capital’s hippest clubs, throbbed with bass. On the dance floor, people tend to wear next to nothing, largely to cope with the heat but also to feel sexy and to attract the wandering eye. Leather shorts, harnesses and sunglasses are par for the course. But more surprising were the number of ties, their Macclesfield, polka dot or tartan designs flashing in the strobe lights.

    The tie might be back.

    The tie, I realised, has become ironically cool.

    “Ties have usually been associated with corporate culture, so when a queer person takes a garment with that type of connotation and applies it to club culture, there’s an element of reclaiming something ordinary and making it theatrical,” says Jordan Wake, a style writer for Vogue. “When I’ve spotted someone wearing a tie on a dancefloor, it’s usually styled with something like a skirt and a pair of heels,” says Wake. “It makes sense that something as simple as a tie would work its way into these spaces.”

    Indeed, a broader shift is emerging, rocketing the humble accessory to new, unfathomable levels of clout. It’s no longer just office workers and club kids; silken, multicoloured neckties are everywhere. The autumn/winter 2026 runways were awash with them. In Milan, Ralph Lauren models wore skinny silk ties; Prada and Dolce & Gabbana dropped tonally complex versions and, in Paris, Louis Vuitton experimented with academic-chic, layering ties beneath knitwear, while Junya Watanabe sent models out wearing multiple ties at once; in London, Paul Smith debuted a range of ties with floral detailing.

    For Spencer Riley, design director at Charles Tyrwhitt, the rise of neckwear is a pushback against the overly casual, work-from-home attire popularised in the early 2020s. People miss dressing up and feeling great. “I remember thinking ties were a thing of the past,” says Riley. “But by 2024, it became clear that ‘status’ was going to become a bigger influence on how men wanted to dress, and the tie started to come back.”

    In innovation terms, unsurprisingly, London is leading the charge. This summer, Harry Styles was never far away from a tie during his Wembley Stadium tour (one, a floral number by the British label JW, celebrated homegrown tailoring); Elle Fanning was deemed a ‘girlboss’ for wearing one at a photocall in the capital last year for new musical drama A Complete Unknown; and 1960s icon Twiggy proved the androgynous look isn’t only for the young, pairing a black smoking jacket with a black tie during Burberry’s autumn/winter 2025 showcase.

    “People are seeing ties on celebrities, influencers and sportsmen and recognising that they can instantly elevate an outfit,” says Riley. “It’s become a fashion trend as much as a formal accessory. For younger men especially, the tie can feel like a relatively simple way of making a statement.”

    It’s also a financial statement: fashion marketplace Depop reported a 31 per cent increase in tie sales in 2025, while the global tie market’s valuation has grown from $3.7bn to $4bn, according to the oddly specific Grand View Research Neckwear Market Report.

    Bold, block colours, and wide 1980s-coded ties are out, with designers preferring subtler designs that nonetheless display character. They might be swaying down catwalks, but it’d be wrong to assume the ironic reclaiming of the tie is tied to sartorial brashness. “Rather than the bright colours and obvious patterns we saw in the past, there’s been a move towards more tonal, textural and complementary styles,” says Riley, pointing to the popularity of Charles Tyrwhitt’s 2026 Grenadine range, which features light, open weave, hand-made pieces. “Grenadine is a great example because it adds interest without overpowering the rest of the outfit.”

    For Gabriella Brick, head of design at Moss Bros, experimentation is key. “The way in which we are styling ties demonstrates how much diversity you can create, whether that’s pairing them with an Italian contrast collar shirt, a button-down Oxford, or even a denim shirt. Ties are no longer just for formal looks.”

    None of this is new, really. The relatively straightforward, contemporary tie is the debauched younger sibling of the elaborate cravat, once de rigueur in high society. These Regency-era staples were a faff to tie, although for the era’s dandies, it was an essential signal of one’s status; from the late 1700s the mess of colour around your neck was a definitive marker of wealth. Workers wore versions cut from cheaper cotton (aristos would baulk at a necktie not made from starched white linen, or some fabulous imported muslin, another signal of their financial status).

Princess Julia, an originator of the movement who says she has gone out and dressed up every night since 1976, is often photographed wearing the tie behind the decks.

    On 25 September 1978, John Peel played Teenage Kicks, the debut single from The Undertones, on his Radio 1 evening show. Two minutes and 28 seconds later, in a brazen breach of BBC protocol, he played the same song for a second time, telling listeners “it doesn’t get much better than this”. 

    I recently had an ‘instant replay’ moment of my own, driving on the Route Napoleon in the French Alps. This glorious road was used for the car chase in Goldeneye, with James Bond (Pierce Brosnan) manhandling an Aston Martin DB5, pursued by Xenia Onatopp in a Ferrari F355. The most spectacular section weaves through a series of steeply stacked hairpins, then clings to the cliff edge, cutting through natural arches in the jagged limestone rock.

    It’s a stretch of tarmac so dramatic, challenging and exhilarating that, when I reached a roundabout, I couldn’t resist turning around and immediately doing it all again. Because it really doesn’t get much better than this, whether you’re driving a blue-blooded supercar or a battery-electric Kia. 

    A new kind of electric performance 

    If that sounds a bit hyperbolic, take note that the EV4 GT is not a common-or-garden Kia. Indeed, with dual motors, all-wheel drive, bigger brakes, adaptive dampers, electronic torque vectoring, Kia’s Virtual Gear Shift system and Pirelli P Zero tyres, it has aspirations to be a proper hot hatchback.

    In recent years, ever-tighter legislation and emissions targets have made such cars into an endangered species. Many have been killed off with no successor in sight, among them the Ford Focus ST, Hyundai i30 N, Renault Megane RS and Honda Civic Type R. For somebody who got his teenage kicks driving hot hatches, this decline has been sad to see. 

    Thankfully, a new breed of electric hot hatches has begun to emerge. If you want something supermini-sized, you can consider the Alpine A290 GTS, Vauxhall Corsa GSE or Peugeot 208 GTI. And at the top end of the market, there is the impressive Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, which resembles a hatchback but has the stature of an SUV.

    Until now, though, no credible EV contender has targeted the hot hatch heartland inhabited by the Volkswagen Golf GTI. That’s where the Kia comes in. 

    Kia EV GT prices and spec

    At £49,345, the EV4 GT is pricier than an entry-level Golf GTI (£41,860) or indeed a Golf R (£46,930). However, being powered by batteries should make for much lower running costs than either – provided you have an EV charger installed at home. 

    Kia also offers its famous seven year, 100,000-mile warranty, plus a long list of standard equipment. The fully loaded GT spec includes intelligent LED headlights, heated and ventilated front seats, 360-degree parking cameras, ambient interior lighting, an electric tailgate and an eight-speaker Harman Kardon sound system. The only option of note is ‘premium’ paint, such as the Blue Flame colour seen here (£650).

    You can tell the GT apart from a regular EV4 by its beefier bumpers, gloss-black trim and neon green brake calipers, which are tucked inside 20-inch alloy wheels. Inside, there’s more neon green on the seatbelts and dashboard, along with alloy pedals and bucket seats trimmed in faux leather and suede. 

    You want numbers? Zero to 62mph takes 5.6 seconds, top speed is 105mph and kerb weight is 2,060kg. The EV-specific stats are 81.4kWh (size of the lithium-ion battery), 128kW (maximum charging speed) 3.4 miles per kWh (energy consumption) and 313 miles (driving range in the official WLTP test).

    The Kia GT story so far

    Kia’s GT badge has been around since the bizarrely punctuated Pro_cee’d GT of 2013. However, apart from the flagship 585hp EV6 GT, the vehicles it was affixed to have been ‘warm’ rather than explicitly hot. They were all overshadowed by sister brand Hyundai’s more extroverted and exciting ‘N’ cars, too.

    This is the first GT model developed from scratch by Manfred Harrer, Kia’s head of R&D since 2025, whose CV includes 14 years at Porsche. It slots into the range between the also-new EV3 GT crossover and EV5 GT SUV, but is the most overtly sporting of the trio. It’s expected to be the best-seller, too – although the EV4 GT exists more to boost Kia’s image than its bottom line. 

    All of which brings us to a hotel car park somewhere north of Nice. The Mediterranean sun is shining, the EV4 GT is brimmed with fresh electrons and the route snakes across its sat-nav screen like tangled strands of spaghetti. Yep, we’ve all had worse days at work.

    Fun for all the family

    Kia’s futuristic ‘Opposites United’ design language works well on an SUV, but looks slab-sided and not particularly sporting here. Still, many will appreciate the GT’s ability to speak softly and carry a 292 horsepower stick. 

    The advantage of that boxy body is plenty of passenger space, helped by the EV4’s ‘skateboard’ platform and flat floor. There’s room for three adults in the back, plus useful stowage in the deep door bins, centre armrest and seat-back pockets. There is no ‘frunk’ and the extra electric motor for the rear axle does rob some boot capacity, however. A total of 377 litres is 58 litres smaller than a standard EV4. 

    Finding a good driving position is easy and the electric seats hug you in the right places. Kia’s in-car tech is also straightforward to use, with a 12.3-inch central touchscreen that syncs wirelessly with your smartphone via Apple CarPlay or Android Auto. The GT even has a data logger to measure your driving performance in real time. 

    Inside the Kia EV4 GT

    Despite the on-board telemetry and the presence of a new GT mode, Kia insists the hottest EV4 is ‘neither an out-and-out performance car, nor a track-day weapon’. The emphasis here, we’re told, is on ‘everyday usable power’ and a ‘familiar, comfortable character’. 

    Accordingly, in the bustle of Nice’s morning rush-hour, the EV4 delivers relaxed, unobtrusive progress. It’s as easy to drive as any electric Kia, with light steering, a hushed soundtrack and decent all-round visibility. There’s also a full complement of electronic driver aids, such as blind-spot monitors and rear cross-traffic assist (to warn of approaching cars when you reverse out of a parking space).

    In Normal mode, the Kia also has a commendably pliant ride, helped by a camera-based system that scans the road surface, preparing the dampers for what lies ahead. And today, as the Cote d’Azur soars majestically upwards into the Alpes-Maritimes, that means some of Europe’s very best driving roads. Route Napoleon, here we come.

    A hotter way to go green

    Push the neon green GT mode toggle on its steering wheel and the EV4 instantly feels energised. Its straight-line performance isn’t scorching by hot hatch standards – the latest Golf R is a second quicker to 62mph –  but the combination of all-wheel drive and an ever-ready 345lb ft of electric torque will slingshot you out of corners. On rural French D-roads, it gets you past dawdling motorhomes quickly and safely, too.

    Kia has set up the GT to be primarily front-driven, in search of traditional hot hatchback handling balance (and more predictable behaviour at the limit, no doubt). Be abrupt with your right foot and all that can overwhelm the front wheels, leading to a scrabble for traction, but such instances are rare. For the most part, the EV4 feels calm and controlled, with limited body-roll and resolute grip from its EV-optimised rubber. 

    Coming back to our Golf R comparison, the Kia has a similar ability to cover ground quickly, making light work of difficult roads. Its steering isn’t the last word in feedback and the regenerative brakes sometimes feel inconsistent. But it’s fun in a grown-up kind of way.

    Like a video game made real

    If you want something more involving/intriguing/immature (delete as appropriate), you can play with the Virtual Gear Shift. Previously seen in the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, this simulates a six-speed manual transmission, accompanied by the snarl of a powerful petrol engine.

    At first, the effect feels rather like playing a video game, but you soon forget the artifice and just enjoy the experience. Leave the VGS in automatic mode and it gives a convincing impression of a twin-clutch auto ’box. Alternatively, you can take control via paddles behind the steering wheel, which are otherwise used to adjust the level of brake energy recovery. The ‘redline’ is at 6,000rpm and you run out of revs at 7,100rpm, causing a lurch as the ‘engine’ bounces off its imaginary limiter. You can’t stall, but well-timed shifts are rewarded with swift, smooth progress.

    As for the soundtrack, a member of Kia’s PR team likened it to the five-cylinder engine in an Audi RS3 and I can’t think of a better comparison. It’s quite different to the hot Hyundai, which has eight virtual gears and sounds more like a turbocharged four.  

    Verdict: Kia EV4 GT

    To paraphrase Mark Twain, reports of the hot hatchback’s death have been greatly exaggerated. Indeed, cars like the EV4 GT offer hope that an electric future doesn’t need to be dull. And if a part of their appeal lies in imitating a petrol car, so be it. If you don’t like the Virtual Gear Shift and five-cylinder fireworks, you can switch them off. 

    Ultimately, the EV4 GT isn’t as entertaining as the benchmark Golf GTI, but it’s a quick and accomplished car that delivers on Kia’s goals to be comfortable and usable. If you’re in the market for a family EV and want more than just fuss-free transport and a long warranty, it’s well worth a look. 

    Who knows, you might even find yourself tackling a great road just for the fun of it. If you’re in the area, may I recommend the Route Napoleon? Just allow yourself enough time to drive it twice.

    Olimera Therapeutics is developing treatments for neurodegenerative diseases by targeting toxic protein clusters that existing technologies cannot reach.

    The company is starting with Parkinson’s disease, but founder Dr Devkee Vadukul told City AM its approach could eventually be applied across several conditions in which toxic proteins accumulate.

    The Santander X funding will go towards incorporation and other costs needed to de-risk the business, as it moves towards that development.

    “The next stage of growth will be to incorporate and build out the team”, Vadukul said. “We are very excited for this to hit the ground running”.

    Within the next few years, the company hopes to be in a position to raise its seed round.

    After more than 14 years working as a midwife, Peripear co-founder Nina spotted a gap between medical evidence and what was actually available in the delivery room.

    Around nine in 10 people who give birth vaginally experience some form of perineal trauma, she said.     On the internet, no one knows you’re a cat. But The Algorithm almost certainly knows if you’re a cat owner, and it will increasingly serve you content aimed at keeping your housebound feline entertained. Welcome to the YouTube phenomenon of Cat TV, a peculiar niche of video streaming whose primary audience (one has to assume) are crepuscular predators with names like Socks, Mr Biscuits and Santa Paws.

    Like most internet phenomena, the origins of Cat TV are a mix of blind luck and ingenuity. One of the genre’s most popular content creators, who was at the forefront of the nascent industry some 10 years ago, is Cornwall-based amateur wildlife photographer Paul Dinning. His YouTube page describes an initial plan to film local bird species for the benefit of other nature lovers, which suddenly blew up when he experimented with the title Videos for Cats. Dinning’s account now has 832,000 subscribers and his most popular videos have amassed millions of views (his 10-minute piece about Cadgwith Cove has not yet broken the internet in quite the same way).

    Jasper the half-Bengal juvenile cat is fixated

    The content itself is unsurprising, for humans at least. I have a half-Bengal juvenile cat called Jasper who is fixated by these eight-hour long videos, filmed in static close-up, of cats, mice and squirrels nibbling at treats on feeder tables. As far as Jasper is concerned, these strange exercises are a high watermark of on-screen entertainment, second only to televised football, where occasional displays of metronomic passing in the mould of early-period Guardiola are known to activate his hunting instincts to such an extent he ends up body-slamming our flatscreen.

    I’m less interested in the psychology of pets, however, than I am the motivation of the creators. A quick scroll of YouTube suggests this cottage industry may be more of a tower block. It turns out amateur enthusiasts like Dinning are the exception rather than the rule of Cat TV. If his early experiments in the form were a happy accident, it didn’t take long for the entrepreneurial twitchers of the internet to realise these recordings represent a simple way to capture a small slice of the attention economy.

    Play Video

    “These videos do well because YouTube ranks them on watch time,” says Adam Jones, the co-founder of social-first video production company Trendy Grandad. “If you watch 30 seconds, that feeds a bad sign into an algorithm. But if you watch five hours of it, that’s a great sign for the algorithm. It’s a good earner in terms of advertising revenue, and people do it to build up watch time and subscribers, which allows them to monetise other content later on. Essentially you’re farming watch time.”

    ‘Cat TV is more cut throat than you would ever imagine‘

    This may explain why, after efforts to contact a large number of the accounts behind these videos, I received only one fairly cryptic response. “The world of Cat TV is probably more surprising and cut throat than you would ever imagine,” said an established creator in the field, who would speak only under the shadow of anonymity. “Due to this I am quite private about what I reveal about myself or my processes.” My follow-up questions went unanswered.

    One positive we can draw from the Cat TV industry is that it does not yet appear to have been eaten up by AI: the majority of the videos are real films of critters. Content produced by channels with names such as Birder King and Cat Games have racked up millions of views, but search traffic is dominated by a relatively small number of players.

    I came across half a dozen accounts struggling to succeed with this traffic fishing approach, with their videos only reaching the hundreds or low thousands of viewers, and in some cases far less. Zoë Glatt, a digital ethnographer at LSE, pointed out that while this type of content “may seem like an easy way to make a quick buck, research shows it is exceptionally hard to build a following and generate sustainable revenue as a content creator, especially in oversaturated content verticals with a low barrier to entry”.

    Perhaps it’s only fitting that content designed for predators, whose natural bloodlust has yet to be bred out of them despite four thousand years of domestication, has given rise to a behind-the-scenes industry just as savage. Beneath the bright eyes and fur, there are always claws.

    On this day, the 1st October, in 1969, Concorde first showed off its real party trick, writes Eliot Wilson in the latest instalment of his on this day series

    It was unusually windy around Toulouse on Wednesday 1 October 1969, the vent d’Autan blowing from the south-east. Its unpredictable gusts and changes in air pressure could drive people insane. Quand l’autan boufa, les bous d’Albi dancent, said the old Occitan proverb. When the Autan blows, the madmen of Albi dance.

    At Toulouse-Blagnac Airport that morning, André Turcat hoped the winds would drop. Nearly 48, he had served with the Armée de l’Air, flying transport aircraft in Indochina before training as a test pilot. Turcat had overseen the experimental phase of the Nord 1500 Griffon ramjet-powered interceptor, and in 1959 he had broken the world speed record over 100km, at an average of 1,021 mph.

    When the Griffon programme ended, Turcat left the air force for Sud Aviation, the state-owned aircraft manufacturer, just as it was about to embark on a joint venture with the British Aircraft Corporation (BAC). BAC and Sud Aviation had both been working on concepts for a supersonic passenger jet; Britain had applied to join the Common Market, while Sud Aviation needed modern large jet engines.

    The result, in November 1962, was a formal international agreement, signed in London by minister of aviation Julian Amery and Geoffrey de Courcel, ambassador of the French Republic. The two companies would develop a supersonic commercial airliner: at a subsequent press conference, the project was first dubbed “Concorde”.

    British pride had taken a knock. In the 1950s, its aeronautical industry had bristled with great names: Vickers-Armstrongs, de Havilland, English Electric, Avro, Hawker Siddeley, Gloster, Bristol, Fairey, Handley Page, Blackburn. And this rich array produced some of the best aircraft in the world.

    The Gloster Meteor had been beaten to the punch as the first operational jet fighter by the Messerschmitt Me-262 by only days in 1944; the de Havilland Comet became the world’s first commercial jet airliner in 1952; and Britain’s nuclear strike force the “V-bombers” – the Vickers Valiant, the Avro Vulcan and the Handley Page Victor – were sophisticated and distinctive aircraft.

    By the 1960s, it had all changed. Manufacturers were herded into the British Aircraft Corporation, its head office at the top of 100 Pall Mall. While it was partnering with Sud Aviation on Concorde, its hopes of ongoing military orders rested on the supersonic strike aircraft TSR-2. The aircraft would succumb to financial constraints and inter-Service rivalry, and was cancelled in 1965. Sir Sydney Camm, designer of the Hawker Hurricane, remarked mordantly: “All modern aircraft have four dimensions: span, length, height and politics. TSR-2 simply got the first three right.”

    Concord or Concorde?

    But there was Concorde. Or Concord? Shortly after the name was announced, President de Gaulle had vetoed the UK’s first application to join the Common Market, though his carefully worded speech never explicitly said “non”. Prime Minister Harold Macmillan, witty and cutting but secretly sensitive, pointedly dropped the “e” and preferred the standard English word ”concord”: agreement, harmony, union.

    It bore more than a little irony: Macmillan had been minister resident in Algiers during the Second World War, where de Gaulle based the Free French headquarters for a time, and knew his prickly hauteur. In 1969, the minister of technology, Anthony Wedgwood Benn, announced in Toulouse he would return the name to “Concorde”, explaining “E stands for excellence, for England, for Europe and for the Entente Cordiale”. Macmillan was reliably funnier than Wedgie.

    Concorde was like nothing aviation had seen before. Its narrow fuselage allowed for only four seats abreast, and a total capacity of between 92 and 128 passengers, but its delta wing and quartet of Rolls Royce/Snecma turbojets allowed it to cruise at twice the speed of sound for three-quarters of a transatlantic flight. Journey times fell by more than half.

    The construction of two prototypes began in 1965. Sud Aviation built 001 at its huge plant at Blagnac Airport, while 002 was manufactured by the BAC Filton Division outside Bristol. The revolutionary and futuristic project caught the imagination, and within four years the consortium had received provisional orders for 74 aircraft from 16 airlines.

    Breaking the sound barrier

    Concorde 001 made its first flight from Toulouse on 1 March 1969 with Turcat at the controls. Legendary test pilot Brian Trubshaw flew 002 on her maiden flight on 9 April from Filton to RAF Fairford. He commented, “It was wizard – a cool, calm and collected operation”. But it was over Toulouse, today in 1969, that Turcat demonstrated Concorde’s real party trick.

    For the first time, Concorde pushed effortlessly through the sound barrier, flying at around 690 mph for nine minutes without seeming out of breath. “All was perfectly calm,” Turcat told reporters afterwards over a glass of champagne. “The Concorde seems made for supersonic flight.” Deliveries of the aircraft would be in late 1973 or early 1974. The world of aviation had changed.

    Or had it? Concorde would suffer a series of grievous wounds. The cost was spiralling, ending up six times as high as projected, £23bn by 1977. The energy crisis following the Yom Kippur War in 1973 highlighted Concorde’s thirst and the efficiency of slower, larger, wide-bodied aircraft.

    But the coup de grâce was the very thing that made Concorde unique: in April 1973, concerned about pollution, take-off noise and the aircraft’s sonic boom, the Federal Aviation Administration banned supersonic flight over US territory. In anticipation, Air Canada, United Airlines, TWA, Pan Am, American Airlines, Eastern Airlines, Braniff and Continental Airlines had all cancelled their orders: 42 aircraft, more than half the total.

    Concorde was not dead, but it would never change the face of flying. Only 20 would be built, and in the hands of British Airways and Air France they become an icon of luxury and privilege. BA’s Heathrow to JFK flight was promoted with the slogan “Arrive before you leave”: it took off at 10.30 am and it was wheels down in New York at 8.30 am local time. A classy trick, an astonishing achievement of engineering, but that was what Concorde would remain.

    • Cocktail order: A protein shake from Joe & the Juice, I’m afraid
    • Favourite book: Meditations by Marcus Aurelius

    What was your first job?

    Selling vaccines to medical practitioners, long before vaccines became a dinner party topic. Turns out the hardest sell in the world is prevention, because nobody ever thanks you for the disease they didn’t get. Everything I know about marketing intangible value, I learned in a GP’s waiting room.

    What was your first role in the City?

    This one, strictly speaking. Although if you’ll grant me Canary Wharf as the City’s younger, taller cousin, I was global head of media and marketing innovation in a previous life.

    When did you know you wanted to build a career in the City/banking?

    I studied chemistry, which is essentially the study of what happens when two things that shouldn’t work together do. Then vaccines, then a stint in advertising, then a chow-mein of a career in banking across Asia-Pacific, Middle East and London. I’m not sure I ever decided on a career so much as kept following the more interesting.

    What’s one thing you love about the City of London?

    The density of unimaginable juxtaposition. You can walk five minutes and pass a Roman wall, a Wren church and three people building AI agents in a basement. Two thousand years of continuous reinvention inside a single square mile.

    And one thing you would change?

    The majority of the City runs almost entirely on league tables, titles and promotions, and almost not at all on whether the work was any good. I’d also retire the belief that seriousness and imagination are opposites. The city still dresses its best ideas in the dullest jargon. It’s refreshing to see how Lloyds is breaking that mould everyday. 

    What’s been your most memorable business lunch?

    Meeting Tim Berners-Lee. He gave the web away rather than monetising it, which is arguably the most consequential marketing decision in history and the precise opposite of what any of us would have advised him to do.

    And any business faux pas?

    I did a short stint in advertising in the days of proofs and bromides. We published a full sale advert with the client’s logo missing. Fallen clean off. We rang them and explained, with total conviction, that it was the teaser phase of the campaign, and they loved it. I’ve been suspicious of confident explanations ever since, including my own.

    What’s been your proudest moment?

    Successfully refreshing a 250-year-old brand in Lloyds and a 350-year-old brand in Scottish Widows in the same year. Making them ready for the app and AI economies and everything that follows. 

    And who do you look up to?

    I run my career like a business, which means I have a personal board of directors. Five of them: three women, two men, four older than me and one younger. I go to them when I’m stuck. They’d rather not be named, which is precisely why the arrangement works.

    What’s the best career advice you’ve ever been given?

    Uncertainty is the price of an interesting career. The certain jobs are rarely the interesting ones, and certainty is usually what a role feels like just before it becomes irrelevant.

    And the worst?

    “Stay in your lane.” Everything worthwhile I’ve done has happened in the gap between two lanes. Or an interesting never-trodden lane. 

    Are you optimistic for the year ahead?

    Yes, and for an unfashionable reason. All our experiments in AI and emerging tech points to the fact that augmentation is what will win, and I am fortunate to work with brilliant minds that are taking the lead in the space. 

    We’re going for lunch, and you’re picking. Where are we going?

    Fish katsu curry takeaway from Deli-Box near St Paul’s on a nippy day, finished on a park bench nearby to watch the world hurry by. Unglamorous, perfect, and you’re back at your desk in 25 minutes.

    And if we’re grabbing a drink after work?

    A neighbourhood boot camp, or a protein shake at Joe & the Juice. I don’t drink, so I’ve quietly swapped the pub round for burpees. Aspirational or antisocial, depending who you ask.

    Where’s home during the week?

    South-west London, deep in nappy valley.

    And where might we find you at the weekend?

    Same place, usually on a bike. I commute on a Genesis, and when mine was stolen I tracked down the last one in the country at a hundred-year-old shop in Ipswich and went to collect it in person. Best day I’d had in months. And now I try to use it as often as I can. 

    You’ve got a well-deserved two weeks off. Where are you going and who with?

    Family, and Luna the dog, who is entirely non-negotiable. Which means the New Forest or Cornwall rather than anywhere requiring a passport and a kennel.

    Britain’s AI minister has ordered changes to government guidance that urged civil servants to limit their use of AI, saying it failed to reflect ministers’ ambitions to ramp up adoption across Whitehall.

    Kanishka Narayan said guidance published last week had now been updated after it advised government workers to use AI only when necessary, choose smaller models and keep prompts to a minimum to cut energy use and costs.

    “Being environmentally conscious and keeping an eye on running costs is, of course, important – but so is encouraging AI adoption and scaling up its use across the public sector”, Narayan said on X.

    “This advice has been updated and we are reviewing similar pages to reflect the fullness of our ambition for the UK”.

    It comes just days after government guidance attracted attention for telling civil servants there was no need to thank AI chatbots, alongside recommendations to use lighter models such as Gemini Flash rather than Gemini Pro and GPT Instant instead of GPT Thinking.

    The guidance said AI uses more energy and resources than conventional software and told staff to consider whether a spreadsheet or search engine could do the job instead.

    Civil servants were also advised to keep prompts “short, clear and direct”, use as few prompts as possible and only turn to AI when needed,

    The latest version instead puts greater emphasis on responsible use rather than discouraging unnecessary use.

    It tells civil servants they remain responsible for their work when using AI and must check its output for inaccuracies, bias or unfairness.

    Staff are also warned to protect sensitive information and use systems provided by their departments for government work.

    “You are responsible for any content or decisions you make using AI”, the new advice says, telling officials to use their own judgement and be prepared to explain decisions made with the technology.

    The change highlights the balancing act facing ministers as they push AI deeper into government while trying to control the risks and costs that come with it.

    Whitehall’s AI push

    The change in direction comes as the government looks to accelerate AI adoption across the public sector, an area that now falls directly within his ministerial responsibilities. Minister Narayan’s brief covers both the government’s AI strategy and public sector adoption.

    Existing government guidance already encourages civil servants to explore how generative AI could improve their work, while warning them not to enter sensitive or personal information and to check outputs for misinformation and bias.

    A government AI playbook published last year similarly set out ten principles for the use of the technology across Whitehall, covering how officials should select, buy and deploy AI safely.

    But the push to accelerate adoption has come alongside concerns over how quickly AI is being introduced into public services and whether sufficient human oversight remains in place.

    The government’s Responsible AI Advisory Panel discussed the need for effective coordination across Whitehall at its latest meeting in September as departments expand their use of the technology.

    Narayan has nevertheless made expanding adoption a central part of his brief, arguing that Britain should develop and deploy advanced AI rather than allow the next technological shift to happen elsewhere.

    Andy Burnham’s “costly” policy agenda and the resurgent threat of inflation are weighing on investors’ appetite for the UK, according to a closely-watched survey of top money managers, which also revealed waning hopes of a rebound in London’s IPO market this year.

    Berenberg’s Investor Barometer, which polled 300 international investors managing a combined $1 trillion, found that 40 per cent pointed to policy decisions as the biggest risk to Britain’s economy, unchanged from the last poll despite a change of government.

    The findings highlight a “continuing lack of confidence in the current administration’s long-term fiscal framework”, authors of the study wrote, despite the UK boasting the most ambitious deficit reduction path of any G7 economy.

    “New Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s costly initial ambitions kept government policy at the top of the list of investor concerns,” Berenberg chief UK economist Andrew Wishart said. “Burnham and the Chancellor have since conceded that higher spending is the wrong choice when borrowing and the tax burden are already problematically high, which gives us some reassurance that they will avoid a major policy error.”

    Investors also raised concerns over inflation’s threat to UK growth. Double the number of asset managers said they were worried about the pace of price rises, which remains well above the Bank of England’s two per cent target, amid the ongoing war in Iran.

    Inflation is expected to top four per cent early next year, as higher energy costs from the Middle East conflict start to appear on household bills and filter into the wider economy.

    Investors expect IPO dearth to continue

    Separately, the temperature check showed just 32 per cent of money managers expect IPO activity to pick up in the next 12 months. The figure, down from 63 per cent from the last barometer six months ago, comes after a barren run of debuts continuing into 2026.

    Uzbekistan’s national investment fund, Uznif, became the only IPO of note this year when it listed a 30 per cent stake on the London and Tashkent stock exchanges in May. But the UK’s flagship bourse was given a shot in the arm last month when African payments firm Airtel Money announced plans for a £5.3bn IPO, in what could be London’s biggest primary capital raise in five years.

    Piers Hillier, chief investment officer at Jupiter, said a credible IPO revival “could make the FTSE a more varied opportunity set for active investors”.

    “UK valuations remain low both to history and other markets, evidenced by the current M&A activity, buybacks and capital returns,” he said. “The UK market has actually been highly divided: large international companies and areas such as mining, defence and financials have performed strongly while many domestically exposed companies have been overlooked.”

    Despite pessimism over the UK’s IPO revival, appetite to participate in big ticket debuts rose, particularly among UK portfolio managers.  Some 24 per cent of investors reported a strong or very strong appetite to participate in IPOs, up from 16 per cent in the spring. More than half of UK-only mandated investment managers want to be involved in IPOs, a sharp uptick.

    Labour conference parties, the Guinness revolution and the DWP response to the triple lock kibosh; catch up on the latest gossip in this week’s The Capitalist

    LABOUR PARTY PARTIES

    Labour supporters want you to know they had a good time in Liverpool. Potential London mayoral candidate Dawn Butler once again threw a Jamaican-themed bash at a local nightclub where MPs including Sarah Sackman, a top barrister, and others were spotted getting in the groove. 

    Ex-Prime Minister hopeful Al Carns was spotted both leading a warm-up at a Labour MP football match against journalists and getting his SAS-built rigs out after a swim off the Mersey. Emily Thornberry also sang at Irish Labour’s party while Angela Rayner spun DJ decks at Labour List’s party. 

    But between the laughs, sports and songs at the Labour Party conference, there were glimpses of despair. 

    Burnham donors and businessmen Sacha Lord and Lord Waheed Alli enjoyed a private lunch together on the first day. It’s impossible not to put that against the context of Reform UK’s mega £72m donation declarations. Relationships with the media are also in the spotlight. A journalist from The Sun was banned from playing against MPs in a football match at Everton FC’s Goodison Park. Remember, The Sun has never backed the wrong horse at general elections. And you can sniff bosses’ unease just a month from a “challenging” Budget. 

    HSBC UK’s chief executive David Lindberg shared a panel with the Treasury minister Emma Reynolds amid swirling rumours that banks could be targeted with higher levies. Zoë Yujnovich, chief executive of National Grid, was on the same panel, a day before the Prime Minister announced he would create a state-owned company for grid connections. 

    Andy Burnham has made an effort to keep his political honeymoon alive but for how much longer can things hold together before fragile relationships – with donors, the media, business and eventually voters – start crumbling?

    TRIPLE LOCK ROCK

    After the Prime Minister announced on Tuesday that Labour was planning to scrap the triple lock, many questions quickly arose. Apparently for the Department for Work and Pensions too. Shortly after the end of the speech in which the policy was pitched (around 15:00), the DWP emailed press (15:47) to arrange a briefing (for 4:30pm) to “answer any technical questions”. Unfortunately (come 16:07), the DWP promptly emailed again to announce the briefing was now cancelled. We guess some questions are easier left unanswered…

    GUINNESS COMES FOR TEATIME

    The Irish aren’t famous for their love of British traditions, but one Irish bar is trying to change that with a rather radical proposition. As of this week, Londoners can enjoy a ‘Guinness Afternoon Tea’ every Saturday at Homeboy in Islington, an offering the Irish bar is calling a “world first”. Featuring smoked salmon on Guinness soda bread, beef and Guinness stew, Guinness cake and, of course, a pint of the black stuff itself, the bar hopes to “reimagine the classic afternoon tea through an Irish lens”. 

    For a £20 premium, punters can also enjoy a “drinks pairing” (Guinness, we assume). It’s pinkies down for this one.
